moments.title: Jesus is crucified in Jerusalem
moments.who: Under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate
moments.body: Jesus of Nazareth, a Galilean Jew, is executed in Jerusalem. His followers — Jews who came to believe he was the Messiah — initially form a sect within Second Temple Judaism. They worship in the Temple and observe Torah.
moments.takeaway: Christianity began as a Jewish movement. The split with mainstream Judaism is decades away.

moments.title: The Council of Jerusalem
moments.who: Peter, James the brother of Jesus, Paul
moments.body: A meeting reported in Acts 15 and Galatians 2 settles whether Gentile converts must be circumcised and keep the Law. The decision (broadly): no, but they should abstain from food sacrificed to idols, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality. Paul's mission to Gentiles is legitimised.

quote.text: It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things.

moments.takeaway: Christianity becomes a religion for Gentiles. This is the structural decision that allows it to become a world religion rather than a Jewish reform movement.

moments.title: Roman destruction of the Temple
moments.who: Titus's legions, ending the First Jewish-Roman War
moments.body: The Second Temple is destroyed. Temple sacrifice ends. Rabbinic Judaism (centred on synagogue, Torah study, halakhah) gradually emerges from the Pharisaic tradition at Yavneh under Yochanan ben Zakkai. Christianity, no longer anchored in Temple worship, continues to spread.
moments.takeaway: After 70 CE, Judaism and Christianity are on diverging trajectories. The Birkat ha-Minim (a synagogue prayer against heretics, late 1st century) is often dated as a marker of communal separation.

moments.title: The Edict of Milan
moments.body: Christianity, illegal and intermittently persecuted for nearly 300 years, is legalised. By 380 (Edict of Thessalonica, Theodosius I) it is the state religion of the Roman Empire.
moments.takeaway: Three centuries from the crucifixion to imperial Christianity. The institutional church, episcopal structure, ecumenical councils all follow.

now.title: Two religions, shared roots
now.body: Christianity now has roughly 2.4 billion adherents, Judaism around 15 million. Both have transformed continuously — the rabbinic tradition through medieval commentators (Rashi, Maimonides), the Hasidic movement (18th century), Reform and Conservative branches (19th); Christianity through monasticism, the Great Schism (1054), Reformation, modern Protestantism, Pentecostalism, post-Vatican II Catholicism.
now.open_questions: Christian-Jewish dialogue is much changed since Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965). But the long history of supersessionism, the Holocaust's role in Christian self-examination, and contemporary politics around Israel remain live.

items.reflection: Religions don't appear fully formed. Christianity took centuries to become 'Christianity' in any institutional sense. Judaism's classical form (rabbinic, Torah-centred, synagogue-based) is also a 1st-century response to crisis. Both faiths are products of history as well as revelation.

moments.title: Baghdad is founded
moments.body: The Abbasid Caliphate builds a new capital on the Tigris, designed as a round city. Within a century it becomes the largest city in the world and the centre of the Islamic Golden Age (roughly 8th-13th centuries).
moments.takeaway: Geography and patronage matter. The Abbasid revolution moved power east, embracing Persian administrative tradition and Greek learning.

moments.title: The House of Wisdom (Bayt al-Hikma)
moments.body: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad sponsors the translation of Greek, Persian, Syriac and Indian texts into Arabic. Hunayn ibn Ishaq translates Galen, Aristotle, Plato. Al-Khwarizmi writes 'Kitab al-Jabr' (the source of the word 'algebra') around 820.

quote.text: Seek knowledge from the cradle to the grave.

moments.takeaway: Greek philosophy and science enter Latin Europe centuries later via Arabic. Without the translation movement, scholastic philosophy would have nothing to work with.

moments.title: Death of Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
moments.body: Ibn Rushd's commentaries on Aristotle become, in Latin translation, foundational for the European universities. Thomas Aquinas refers to him simply as 'the Commentator'. The Latin Averroist movement at Paris in the 13th century is a major intellectual force.
moments.takeaway: Aquinas's Summa Theologiae would be inconceivable without Ibn Rushd. So would Dante's representation of him in the Limbo of the virtuous pagans.

now.title: After the Golden Age
now.body: The 1258 Mongol sack of Baghdad ended Abbasid Baghdad and is often used as a closing marker, though Islamic scholarship continued vibrantly in Cairo, Cordoba, Samarkand, Istanbul, Isfahan. Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal empires continued patronage. The 'decline' narrative is contested by historians like George Saliba, who argues Islamic science continued producing original work well into the early modern period.
now.open_questions: Why did the scientific revolution happen in Europe rather than continuing in the Islamic world? The question has many answers — institutional (the university), political (state competition), economic (Atlantic trade), religious — and no consensus.

items.reflection: Histories of 'Western' philosophy that jump from Aristotle to Aquinas erase a thousand years of Islamic intermediation. The intellectual debt is structural, not decorative.

moments.title: Luther's 95 Theses
moments.who: Martin Luther, Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg
moments.body: On 31 October 1517, Luther posts (or sends — the door-posting is contested) 95 theses for academic disputation, attacking the sale of indulgences by Johann Tetzel. The Theses, in Latin, are translated into German and printed within months. The Reformation begins.

quote.text: Here I stand, I can do no other.
quote.attrib: Luther, reportedly at the Diet of Worms, 1521

moments.takeaway: Without the printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1440) Luther's protest would have been local. With it, his pamphlets reached enormous audiences within months.

moments.title: The Act of Supremacy
moments.body: Henry VIII, refused an annulment by Rome, declares himself Supreme Head of the Church of England. The English Reformation is initially political and dynastic; doctrinal reform follows under Edward VI (1547-1553), reverses under Mary I (1553-1558), and consolidates under Elizabeth I (1558-1603).
moments.takeaway: The Reformation in England was driven by Henry's dynastic crisis as much as by theology. The Elizabethan Settlement is a compromise still visible in the Church of England today.

moments.title: Peace of Westphalia
moments.who: European powers ending the Thirty Years' War
moments.body: The wars of religion that followed the Reformation ended in 1648 with a treaty system that, broadly, accepted confessional diversity and the right of rulers to determine their states' religion (cuius regio, eius religio). It also marks the conventional birth of the modern sovereign state system.
moments.takeaway: Religious toleration emerged from exhaustion, not principle. The political form (the territorial state) was the lasting legacy as much as the theology.

now.title: Five centuries on
now.body: Protestantism is now extremely diverse — Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Pentecostal and many more. The 2017 Reformation 500 commemorations saw Pope Francis travel to Lund, Sweden, for a joint Catholic-Lutheran service — unthinkable a century earlier. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) formally narrowed the original sola fide dispute.
now.open_questions: Was the Reformation the start of secular modernity? Charles Taylor's 'A Secular Age' (2007) argues yes — internalised religion, the disenchantment of nature and the rise of the individual conscience all have Reformation roots. Brad Gregory's 'The Unintended Reformation' (2012) is more critical.

items.reflection: A single Augustinian friar's protest against indulgences split Western Christendom, redrew political maps, and reshaped epistemology. The unintended consequences of doctrinal disputes can be civilisational.

moments.title: Crucifixion of Jesus
moments.who: Jesus of Nazareth, under Pontius Pilate
moments.body: Jesus of Nazareth, a Galilean Jew, is executed in Jerusalem under the Roman prefect Pontius Pilate. His followers — Jews who believed him to be the Messiah — initially form a sect within Second Temple Judaism, worshipping in the Temple and observing Torah.
moments.takeaway: Christianity began as a Jewish movement. The earliest community is in Jerusalem under James the brother of Jesus.

moments.title: Pentecost
moments.body: Acts 2 describes the descent of the Holy Spirit on the disciples 50 days after Passover (the Jewish festival of Shavuot). Peter preaches and around 3,000 are reported baptised. Pentecost is celebrated as the birth of the Church.

quote.text: And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind.

moments.takeaway: The Pentecost narrative frames the Church's mission as universal — speaking in many languages to many nations.

moments.title: Paul's missionary journeys
moments.body: Three major missions across Asia Minor, Greece and beyond. Paul founds and corresponds with churches in Corinth, Thessalonica, Galatia, Philippi, Rome. His letters (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians and others, written 50s CE) are the earliest Christian texts to survive.
moments.takeaway: Paul, originally a persecutor of the church, becomes its most effective missionary. His extension of the message to Gentiles is decisive for Christianity becoming a world religion.

moments.title: Council of Jerusalem
moments.body: Acts 15 and Galatians 2 record the decision that Gentile converts need not be circumcised or observe the full Mosaic Law. The threshold for joining is lowered; Christianity becomes a religion for non-Jews as well as Jews.
moments.takeaway: The structural decision that allows Christianity to spread beyond Judaism.

now.title: From sect to world religion
now.body: Christianity now has around 2.4 billion adherents — the world's largest religion. The earliest decades (30-50 CE) are documented primarily through Paul's letters, the Gospels (written 65-100 CE) and Acts (probably 80s-90s CE). The historical Jesus (E. P. Sanders, Dale Allison) and the historical Paul (N. T. Wright) remain active scholarly fields.
now.open_questions: How quickly did Jesus's followers see him as divine? 'Early high Christology' (Larry Hurtado) argues within months; others see development over decades. The phrase 'Lord Jesus' appears in 1 Corinthians 16:22, written around 53-54 CE.

items.reflection: Within 30 years of Jesus's death, what began as a Jewish messianic movement was operating across the Roman Empire and writing to Gentile congregations. The speed of that early spread is itself a major historical question.

moments.title: Edict of Milan
moments.body: After Constantine's victory at the Milvian Bridge (October 312), he and Licinius issue the Edict of Milan granting religious toleration across the Roman Empire. Christianity, persecuted intermittently for nearly three centuries, becomes legal.
moments.takeaway: Constantine's policy was not yet full imperial sponsorship of Christianity, but the legal change made bishops powerful figures.

moments.title: Council of Nicaea
moments.body: Constantine convenes the first ecumenical council at Nicaea (now İznik, Turkey) to settle the Arian controversy — whether the Son was co-eternal with the Father, or a created being. The Council condemns Arius and produces the Nicene Creed affirming the Son as 'of one substance' (homoousios) with the Father.

quote.text: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of all things visible and invisible.

moments.takeaway: Nicaea did NOT decide the canon of Scripture — a persistent modern myth. It settled the Christological question that defines mainstream Christianity to this day.

moments.title: Council of Constantinople
moments.body: The First Council of Constantinople expanded the Nicene Creed (the version most commonly recited today is technically the 'Niceno-Constantinopolitan' Creed). The Edict of Thessalonica (380) had made Nicene Christianity the state religion of the Roman Empire.
moments.takeaway: By the late 4th century, Nicene Trinitarian Christianity was orthodox state religion. Arianism survived among Germanic peoples (Goths, Vandals) for centuries.

now.title: Nicaea's enduring shape
now.body:
The Nicene Creed remains the most widely shared Christian statement of faith — recited by Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans and many Protestants. The Filioque clause ('and the Son') was added by Western churches in the 6th-11th centuries and became one of the issues splitting Western and Eastern Christianity in 1054.

Dan Brown's 'The Da Vinci Code' (2003) repeated the false claim that Nicaea decided the biblical canon. The 27-book New Testament was settled gradually through the 4th-5th centuries, first listed in its current form by Athanasius's Easter Letter of 367.
now.open_questions: How much of Nicaea was politics, and how much theology? Constantine wanted unity; bishops also wanted theological clarity. Most modern scholars see both motives as real and intertwined.

items.reflection: Christian orthodoxy is shaped by specific councils with specific political pressures. The Trinitarian theology that defines mainstream Christianity was hammered out in the 4th century — not from the New Testament directly but from centuries of theological argument under imperial pressure.

moments.title: Augustine's conversion
moments.body: Augustine, a teacher of rhetoric, describes his conversion in a garden in Milan in August 386. Hearing a child's voice chanting 'tolle lege' ('take and read'), he opens Paul's letter to the Romans and reads. He is baptised by Ambrose, Bishop of Milan, the following Easter (387).
moments.takeaway: Augustine had previously been a Manichaean, then a Neoplatonist. His conversion narrative shapes Christian autobiographical tradition for 1,600 years.

moments.title: Confessions
moments.body: Augustine writes the Confessions — 13 books addressed to God, recounting his spiritual journey from infancy. The form is unprecedented: introspective autobiography as theological argument.

quote.text: Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new.

moments.takeaway: The Confessions invented Christian autobiography. Petrarch, Rousseau, Newman and many others wrote under its influence.

moments.title: City of God
moments.who: Augustine writing after the sack of Rome (410)
moments.body: After Visigothic Alaric sacked Rome in 410, pagans blamed Christianity for the empire's decline. Augustine's massive 'De Civitate Dei contra Paganos' answers: the eternal city is not Rome but the City of God. Earthly empires rise and fall; the spiritual city endures.
moments.takeaway: City of God shapes Western political theology for over a millennium. The two-cities framework underlies medieval church-state debates.

now.title: Augustine's long shadow
now.body:
Augustine (354-430) shaped Western Christianity more than any other thinker after Paul. Doctrines of original sin, predestination, the just war, the Trinity — all bear his imprint. Aquinas extended Augustine; Luther was an Augustinian friar; Jansenism revived Augustine in 17th-century France.

His 'Retractations' (426-427) — a late review of his own works — is itself a striking act of intellectual humility.
now.open_questions: Did Augustine darken Christianity? His doctrines of original sin and predestination were more pessimistic than the Eastern Christian tradition. Modern Catholic and Orthodox theology often returns to pre-Augustinian sources for alternative frameworks.

items.reflection: A single late-Roman bishop's reading of Paul and his own life shaped Christianity for 1,600 years. The Confessions and City of God are still read because Augustine's questions — about will, sin, time, memory and political order — are still the questions Western thinkers ask.

moments.title: Death of Muhammad
moments.body: 8 June 632: Muhammad dies at Medina without naming a clear successor. At Saqifah, Abu Bakr is chosen as the first caliph by a majority of the community. A minority hold that Ali (Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law) had been designated.
moments.takeaway: The succession question is the foundational political issue of Islam. Both Sunni and Shia traditions trace their distinct identities to this moment.

moments.title: Ali's caliphate and the First Fitna
moments.body: After the assassinations of caliphs Umar (644) and Uthman (656), Ali becomes the fourth Rightly-Guided Caliph. He moves the capital from Medina to Kufa. Mu'awiya, governor of Syria and a relative of Uthman, refuses to recognise Ali. The First Fitna (civil war) follows. Ali is assassinated at Kufa in 661.
moments.takeaway: Mu'awiya founds the Umayyad Caliphate, marking the shift to dynastic rule. The Rightly-Guided Caliphate of the four (Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman, Ali) becomes a Sunni reference point.

moments.title: Karbala
moments.who: Husayn ibn Ali and the Umayyad army
moments.body: 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680): Husayn, Ali's son and Muhammad's grandson, is killed at Karbala (in modern Iraq) by Umayyad forces under Yazid I. Husayn's small party (around 72 followers) refused to accept Yazid's rule.

quote.text: Death with dignity is better than life with humiliation.
quote.attrib: Attributed to Husayn ibn Ali at Karbala

moments.takeaway: Karbala defines Shia identity as a community of mourning and resistance. The annual commemoration of Ashura mourns Husayn.

now.title: Sunni-Shia today
now.body:
Sunni Muslims are around 85-90% of the world's 1.9 billion Muslims; Shia around 10-15%. Shia majorities: Iran, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Bahrain. Significant minorities: Lebanon, Yemen, Syria, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Afghanistan, India.

Major Shia branches include Twelvers (the largest), Ismailis (the Aga Khan's community) and Zaydis (Yemen). Sectarian conflict in the 20th-21st centuries (Iran-Iraq War 1980-88, post-2003 Iraq, Syria, Yemen) has often been framed in Sunni-Shia terms — though political and economic factors are usually closer to the surface.
now.open_questions: How political was the original split? Modern historians (Hugh Kennedy, Wilferd Madelung) emphasise its political-dynastic origin; the theological elaboration came later but became inseparable from the identity.

items.reflection: The largest division within Islam began as a political succession dispute and was consolidated by a 7th-century massacre. The political origin doesn't make the theological content less real — but understanding the origin reframes the contemporary politics.

moments.title: Siddhartha Gautama is born
moments.body: Siddhartha Gautama is born to a noble family of the Shakya clan in Lumbini (now in Nepal). Traditional dating put his life around 563-483 BCE; modern scholarship often dates him to around 480-400 BCE.
moments.takeaway: Buddha is not a name but a title — 'awakened one'. There can be (and are said to have been) many Buddhas; the Buddha of our historical period is Siddhartha Gautama.

moments.title: Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
moments.body: After leaving palace life at age 29, Siddhartha studied with teachers, practised severe asceticism for six years, and finally sat in meditation under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya. After 49 days he attained enlightenment, understanding the Four Noble Truths.
moments.takeaway: The Buddha rejected both indulgence and extreme asceticism in favour of a 'Middle Way'.

moments.title: First sermon at Sarnath
moments.who: The Buddha and the five ascetics
moments.body: The Buddha travelled to Sarnath, near Varanasi, where he gave his first sermon — the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, 'Setting the Wheel of Dharma in Motion' — to five former companions. The sangha (monastic community) was founded.

quote.text: Now this, monks, is the noble truth of dukkha.
quote.attrib: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, opening of the Four Noble Truths

moments.takeaway: The Buddha taught for around 45 years before his parinirvana (around 483 or 400 BCE) in Kushinagar. His teachings were transmitted orally for centuries before being written down.

now.title: Two and a half millennia of Buddhism
now.body:
Buddhism is now followed by around 500 million people, mostly in Asia. Theravada dominates South-East Asia and Sri Lanka; Mahayana dominates East Asia; Vajrayana dominates Tibet and Mongolia.

The earliest Buddhist texts (the Pali Canon) were committed to writing around 100 BCE in Sri Lanka. Mahayana sutras (Prajnaparamita, Lotus, Pure Land) emerged from around the 1st century BCE onwards.

The Dalai Lama (the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism) and Thich Nhat Hanh (Vietnamese Zen) shaped modern Buddhism's Western reception in the 20th century.
now.open_questions: When did the Buddha actually live? The traditional and revised datings differ by around 80 years. Texts that look stable were oral for centuries — what we have is the form preserved by later sanghas.

items.reflection: Buddhism began with one person's experience and one sermon to five listeners. 2,500 years later it is a global religion with traditions that the founder might struggle to recognise. The question of what is 'authentically Buddhist' has been live since the Second Council, around 100 years after his death.

moments.title: Rig Veda composed
moments.body: The Rig Veda — 1,028 hymns to deities including Indra, Agni, Soma and Varuna — is composed in early Sanskrit, transmitted orally with extraordinary fidelity. The other three Vedas (Sama, Yajur, Atharva) follow.
moments.takeaway: The Vedas are sruti — 'that which is heard' — the most sacred Hindu texts. They predate all other surviving major religious texts of the world's living religions.

moments.title: Principal Upanishads
moments.body: The Upanishads — philosophical texts attached to the Vedas — develop concepts of atman (self), Brahman (ultimate reality), karma (action and consequence), samsara (rebirth) and moksha (liberation). The Brihadaranyaka and Chandogya are the oldest.

quote.text: Tat tvam asi.

moments.takeaway: The Upanishads inaugurate Indian philosophical inquiry. Their themes — the unity of self and ultimate reality, liberation from rebirth — shape every subsequent Indian religion.

moments.title: Epic and classical period
moments.body: The Mahabharata (including the Bhagavad Gita) and Ramayana — vast epic poems — take written form. The Dharmashastras (including Manusmriti) codify social and ritual duty. The six classical darshanas (philosophical schools) — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta — emerge.
moments.takeaway: What we now call Hinduism is consolidated in this period — a tradition of texts, schools and practices recognising the authority of the Vedas.

now.title: Hinduism in the modern world
now.body:
Hinduism has around 1.2 billion adherents, mostly in India (around 80% of Indians) and Nepal, with significant communities in Bali, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, the UK and the US. The Bhakti movement (medieval), Neo-Vedanta (Vivekananda, 1893 Parliament of Religions in Chicago), and the global yoga movement (20th century) have shaped its modern profile.

Hindu nationalism (Hindutva) as a 20th-21st-century political movement is contested — both about its accuracy as a description of the tradition and about its consequences for India's religious pluralism.
now.open_questions: Is 'Hinduism' a single religion or a family of traditions? The term itself is a modern (largely 19th-century) coinage from the Persian word for the Indus river. Wendy Doniger and others have argued for diversity within the term.

items.reflection: Hinduism is the world's oldest continuously practised major religion. Its founding texts predate the Buddha, Confucius, the Hebrew prophets and the Pre-Socratics. The Upanishads' philosophical questions — about self, reality and liberation — are still alive in contemporary Indian thought.

moments.title: Guru Nanak is born
moments.who: Nanak, in Talwandi (now Nankana Sahib, Pakistan)
moments.body: Born on 15 April 1469 (some traditions place it on the full moon of Kartik in October-November). He grew up in Mughal-era Punjab amid Hindu-Muslim tensions, working as an accountant before his spiritual experience around 1499.
moments.takeaway: Sikh tradition emphasises Nanak's distinctness from both Hindu and Muslim traditions of his time. He is said to have responded to his vision with 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.'

moments.title: Ten human Gurus
moments.body: The ten human Gurus: Nanak (1469-1539), Angad (1539-1552), Amar Das (1552-1574), Ram Das (1574-1581), Arjan (1581-1606, martyred by Mughals), Hargobind (1606-1644), Har Rai (1644-1661), Har Krishan (1661-1664), Tegh Bahadur (1664-1675, martyred), Gobind Singh (1675-1708).
moments.takeaway: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604. The 'martial' tradition emerged under Hargobind in response to Mughal persecution.

moments.title: Founding of the Khalsa
moments.body: Vaisakhi (April) 1699: Guru Gobind Singh asks for volunteers willing to die for the faith. The Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones) step forward. They are initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword) and then themselves initiate the Guru. The Khalsa — community of the 'pure' — is founded.
moments.takeaway: The Khalsa is marked by the Five Ks (Kesh, Kara, Kanga, Kachera, Kirpan). Members take the surnames Singh (lion) for men and Kaur (princess) for women, symbolically equalising caste and gender.

moments.title: Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru
moments.who: Guru Gobind Singh before his death
moments.body: Before his death (from an Afghan assassin's wound), Guru Gobind Singh declares the Guru Granth Sahib — the scripture compiled by Guru Arjan with additions — to be the eternal Guru. There will be no more human Gurus.
moments.takeaway: Scripture as Guru ended succession disputes. The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru, bowed to, awakened in the morning and put to rest at night.

now.title: Sikhism today
now.body:
Sikhism has around 25-30 million adherents, mostly in Punjab (India) and the Sikh diaspora (UK, Canada, US). The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) at Amritsar (built under Guru Arjan) is the central shrine. Daily langar (free communal meal) at the Golden Temple serves around 100,000 people.

Major 20th-century events: Partition (1947) split Punjab and displaced millions; Operation Blue Star (1984) by the Indian army at the Golden Temple, and the assassination of Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguards months later, traumatised the community.
now.open_questions: How should Sikhism relate to Hinduism and Islam? Some scholars frame it as a syncretic movement of medieval Punjab; Sikhs themselves emphasise its distinctness from the start.

items.reflection: Sikhism is the youngest of the major world religions with a clear founder. Its trajectory from Nanak's spiritual vision (1499) to the founding of the Khalsa (1699) to the eternal Guru Granth Sahib (1708) is dense and well-documented — a religion whose origins are not obscured by myth.

moments.title: Aquinas studies under Albert the Great
moments.who: Thomas Aquinas in Paris and Cologne
moments.body: Aquinas (born c. 1225) studies in Paris and Cologne under Albert the Great, one of the leading Aristotelians of the day. His family had tried to prevent him joining the Dominican Order, even imprisoning him for over a year.
moments.takeaway: Aristotle's works had reached Latin Europe in the 12th-13th centuries through Arabic translations from Islamic Spain and Sicily. Reading Aristotle alongside Christian theology was the defining intellectual project of 13th-century Paris.

moments.title: Summa Theologiae
moments.body: Aquinas writes the Summa Theologiae — over 3,000 articles structured as questions and answers — as a teaching text for theology students. It covers God, the Trinity, creation, ethics, Christ, the sacraments and last things. He left it unfinished after a mystical experience on 6 December 1273 led him to stop writing.

quote.text: I cannot. Such things have been revealed to me that all I have written seems to me as so much straw.
quote.attrib: Aquinas, on stopping writing in December 1273

moments.takeaway: The Five Ways — five arguments for God's existence — appear in Summa Theologiae I.2.3, occupying only about a page. The work as a whole runs to millions of words.

moments.title: Canonisation
moments.body: Aquinas was canonised on 18 July 1323, 49 years after his death. He was declared Doctor of the Church in 1567 by Pius V. Leo XIII's encyclical Aeterni Patris (1879) made Thomism the philosophical basis of Catholic seminary education.
moments.takeaway: Aquinas's status grew steadily from the 14th to the 19th centuries. He is the only theologian whose work was placed on the altar at the Council of Trent alongside the Bible.

now.title: Aquinas in modern thought
now.body:
Thomism (the school of philosophy following Aquinas) remains the largest tradition in Catholic philosophy. Neo-Thomism (Étienne Gilson, Jacques Maritain in the 20th century) and Analytical Thomism (Anthony Kenny, John Haldane) are contemporary developments.

Aquinas's Five Ways are part of every A-level Religious Studies syllabus. His natural law ethics shapes Catholic moral teaching on issues from contraception to euthanasia.
now.open_questions: Is Aquinas's synthesis of Aristotle and Christian theology stable? Reformers like Luther argued no. 20th-century theologians (Karl Barth) preferred a sharper separation. Catholic theology continues to find his framework productive.

items.reflection: A 13th-century Dominican friar's project — synthesising Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology — became the dominant framework for Catholic thought for 750 years. The Five Ways are taught in modern philosophy classes; the natural law ethics shapes contemporary debate. Few thinkers have a longer reach.

moments.title: Luther's 95 Theses
moments.who: Martin Luther, Augustinian friar and professor at Wittenberg
moments.body: On 31 October 1517, Luther posts (or sends — the door-posting is contested) 95 theses for academic disputation, attacking the sale of indulgences by Johann Tetzel. The Theses, in Latin, are translated into German and printed within months. The Reformation begins.

quote.text: Here I stand, I can do no other.
quote.attrib: Luther, reportedly at the Diet of Worms, 1521

moments.takeaway: Without the printing press (Gutenberg, c. 1440) Luther's protest would have been local. With it, his pamphlets reached enormous audiences within months.

moments.title: Diet of Worms
moments.who: Luther before Holy Roman Emperor Charles V
moments.body: April 1521: Luther is summoned to the Imperial Diet at Worms to recant. He refuses, citing Scripture and conscience. The Edict of Worms declares him an outlaw. Frederick the Wise of Saxony 'kidnaps' him to Wartburg Castle for protection, where Luther translates the New Testament into German (published 1522).
moments.takeaway: Luther's German Bible became one of the most influential books in shaping the German language.

moments.title: Augsburg Confession to Westphalia
moments.body: The Augsburg Confession (1530) sets out Lutheran doctrine. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) recognises Lutheranism in the Empire under 'cuius regio, eius religio'. Wars of religion across Europe culminate in the Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) and the Peace of Westphalia.
moments.takeaway: Religious toleration emerged from exhaustion, not principle. Westphalia established the modern state system.

now.title: Five centuries on
now.body: Protestantism is now extremely diverse — Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican, Baptist, Pentecostal and many more — with around 900 million adherents worldwide. The 2017 Reformation 500 commemorations saw Pope Francis travel to Lund, Sweden, for a joint Catholic-Lutheran service — unthinkable a century earlier. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) formally narrowed the original sola fide dispute.
now.open_questions: Was the Reformation the start of secular modernity? Charles Taylor's 'A Secular Age' (2007) argues yes — internalised religion, the disenchantment of nature and the rise of the individual conscience all have Reformation roots. Brad Gregory's 'The Unintended Reformation' (2012) is more critical.

items.reflection: A single Augustinian friar's protest against indulgences split Western Christendom, redrew political maps, and reshaped epistemology. The unintended consequences of doctrinal disputes can be civilisational.

moments.title: Henry's 'Great Matter'
moments.who: Henry VIII, Catherine of Aragon, Pope Clement VII
moments.body: Henry, without a male heir from Catherine of Aragon, seeks annulment from Pope Clement VII. Clement is effectively a prisoner of Catherine's nephew, Emperor Charles V, after the 1527 Sack of Rome and cannot grant it. Henry breaks with Rome.
moments.takeaway: The English Reformation begins as a dynastic crisis, not a doctrinal revolt. Henry remained theologically conservative throughout his reign.

moments.title: Acts of Parliament
moments.who: Thomas Cromwell and the Reformation Parliament
moments.body: Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) declares England an 'empire' subject to no foreign jurisdiction. Cranmer annuls Henry's marriage to Catherine (May 1533). Act of Supremacy (3 November 1534) declares the king 'Supreme Head' of the Church of England.

quote.text: The King's good servant, but God's first.

moments.takeaway: Thomas More and John Fisher refused the Oath of Succession and were executed in 1535. The Reformation in England was enacted by statute, not by popular preaching.

moments.title: Settlements and reversals
moments.who: Edward VI, Mary I, Elizabeth I
moments.body: Edward VI (1547-1553) introduced Reformed doctrine (1549 and 1552 Books of Common Prayer). Mary I (1553-1558) restored Catholicism and burned around 280 Protestants. Elizabeth I (1558-1603) established the Elizabethan Settlement of 1559 — a deliberately broad via media between Catholic and Reformed.
moments.takeaway: The English Reformation took 25 years and four reversals to settle. The 'Anglican' tradition emerged from this contested process.

now.title: An established church
now.body:
The Church of England remains the established church in England. The monarch is still Supreme Governor (a softer 1559 formulation than Henry's 'Supreme Head'). The Anglican Communion now has around 85 million members worldwide, with strong growth in Africa.

Catholic emancipation came only in 1829. The Oxford Movement (1830s onwards) revived Catholic elements within Anglicanism. The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999) and ARCIC (Anglican-Roman Catholic International Commission) dialogues have narrowed historic disputes.
now.open_questions: Was the English Reformation Henry's project that escaped him, or part of a wider European movement? Eamon Duffy's 'Stripping of the Altars' (1992) argued the Reformation was imposed against popular reluctance; A. G. Dickens's earlier 'English Reformation' (1964) had emphasised popular Protestant momentum.

items.reflection: The Church of England is the world's clearest case of a religious settlement designed by political compromise. Five centuries on, its modern shape — episcopal, vernacular, doctrinally broad — is recognisably the 1559 settlement, with all the ambiguities that entails.

moments.title: John XXIII announces a council
moments.body: 25 January 1959: less than three months after his election, John XXIII surprises the Roman Curia by announcing a new ecumenical council — the first since Vatican I (1869-70). He uses the word 'aggiornamento' (updating) to describe its purpose.
moments.takeaway: The decision broke with expectations of a transitional papacy. John XXIII (then aged 77) opened the Church to engagement with modernity.

moments.title: Vatican II
moments.who: Around 2,500 bishops, observers from other Christian traditions
moments.body: Second Vatican Council met in four sessions from 11 October 1962 to 8 December 1965 (under John XXIII and his successor Paul VI). Major documents: Lumen Gentium (the Church), Dei Verbum (Scripture and revelation), Sacrosanctum Concilium (liturgy — vernacular Mass), Gaudium et Spes (the Church in the modern world), Nostra Aetate (relations with non-Christian religions), Dignitatis Humanae (religious freedom).

quote.text: The joys and the hopes, the griefs and the anxieties of the men of this age, especially those who are poor or in any way afflicted, these are the joys and hopes, the griefs and anxieties of the followers of Christ.

moments.takeaway: Nostra Aetate explicitly rejected the charge of collective Jewish guilt for the death of Jesus — a major rapprochement after the Holocaust.

now.title: Reception and secularisation
now.body:
Vatican II's reception remains contested. 'Spirit of Vatican II' progressives emphasised further reform; 'hermeneutic of continuity' conservatives (Joseph Ratzinger / Benedict XVI) emphasised the Council's continuity with tradition.

Western European Catholicism has declined sharply since the 1960s. UK 2021 Census: Christian affiliation fell from 72% (2001) to 46% (2021); 'no religion' rose from 15% to 37%. Mass attendance has fallen even faster than affiliation. Secularisation theory (Bryan Wilson, Peter Berger) and its critics (José Casanova, Charles Taylor) have debated whether decline is universal or local.
now.open_questions: Did Vatican II cause Catholic decline, or fail to prevent it? Conservative and progressive readings give different answers. Comparing post-conciliar Catholic decline with similar declines in other Western Christian traditions suggests broader social forces are at work.

items.reflection: Vatican II was the largest event in modern Catholic history — a deliberate engagement with modernity by the institution that had spent the previous century resisting it. Its long-term effects are still being worked out as the broader landscape of religion in Western societies continues to shift.

moments.title: Growing estrangement
moments.body: The Western and Eastern Christian halves of the Roman Empire diverge linguistically (Latin vs Greek), liturgically and politically. The Western addition of 'Filioque' to the Nicene Creed (i.e. the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father 'and the Son'), the question of papal primacy, and disputes over leavened/unleavened bread accumulate.
moments.takeaway: The split was a long process, not a single event. Disputes had been mounting for centuries.

moments.title: Mutual excommunications
moments.who: Cardinal Humbert and Patriarch Michael Cerularius
moments.body: 16 July 1054: Cardinal Humbert lays a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia. Patriarch Cerularius reciprocates. Both excommunications were personally directed and arguably without authority, but they came to symbolise the institutional schism.
moments.takeaway: Pope Leo IX had already died (April 1054), arguably invalidating Humbert's mandate.

moments.title: Sack of Constantinople
moments.body: 13 April 1204: Western crusaders sack Constantinople, profaning Hagia Sophia, looting relics. The Latin Empire is established briefly. The bitterness this caused made reunion attempts (Lyon 1274, Florence 1439) politically untenable.

quote.text: Forgive us our trespasses.
quote.attrib: Pope John Paul II, apology to Eastern Orthodox Christians, 2001

moments.takeaway: The 1204 sack is often cited as the moment the schism became unbridgeable. The 1964 mutual lifting of the 1054 excommunications by Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras was a partial reconciliation.

now.title: Two churches, one Christ
now.body: Catholic and Orthodox churches share most theology, sacraments and creedal structure but remain organisationally separate. Around 1.3 billion Catholics, 220 million Orthodox. Ecumenical dialogue resumed after Vatican II (1962-65). The 2016 Pan-Orthodox Council and the 2018-19 Ukrainian Orthodox autocephaly dispute reveal ongoing internal Orthodox tensions.
now.open_questions: Can they reunite? Theological consensus on most points is closer than many imagine. Papal primacy remains the major obstacle. Mark Mazower and Diarmaid MacCulloch have explored the history.

items.reflection: The two largest branches of Christianity have lived alongside each other for nearly a thousand years without communion. The accumulated cultural divergence is now itself part of the divide — even if formal reunion were possible, two parallel histories cannot be erased.

moments.title: Abraham's covenant
moments.body: Genesis records God's covenant with Abraham — promise of land, descendants, and blessing to the nations. Sealed by circumcision (Genesis 17). The Akedah (binding of Isaac, Genesis 22) is foundational test text.
moments.takeaway: Abrahamic monotheism is the common origin claimed by Judaism, Christianity and Islam — though each interprets the covenant differently.

moments.title: Exodus and Sinai
moments.body: Exodus from Egyptian slavery (Passover origin), forty years in the wilderness, the giving of the Torah at Sinai. The Decalogue (Ten Commandments, Exodus 20). Modern archaeology finds no direct evidence of mass exodus but the narrative is foundational.
moments.takeaway: Pesach (Passover) remains the central Jewish festival. The story is retold every year — 'In each generation, every person must regard themselves as having gone out from Egypt'.

moments.title: Davidic kingdom and Solomon's Temple
moments.body: David unifies Israel and Judah; Solomon builds the First Temple in Jerusalem (c. 957 BCE). Temple worship — sacrifice, priesthood, festivals — becomes central. The kingdom splits after Solomon (922 BCE).
moments.takeaway: The Temple is the centre of biblical Judaism. Its later destructions (586 BCE, 70 CE) reshape what Judaism becomes.

now.title: Judaism's foundational claims
now.body: Modern Judaism continues to centre on covenant, Torah and community. Reform, Conservative, Orthodox and Reconstructionist branches share these foundations even where they differ on practice. The State of Israel (founded 1948) raised the relationship between Judaism, peoplehood and political sovereignty in new forms.
now.open_questions: What is the historical relationship to the biblical narrative? Mainstream scholarship treats much of Genesis-Joshua as constructed memory rather than literal history. This shifts how the covenant tradition is understood but not its religious force.

items.reflection: The Abrahamic-covenant framework is foundational to half the world's religious population — Jews, Christians, Muslims all trace lineage to it. Understanding the family resemblance is essential to understanding any of the three.

moments.title: Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem
moments.body: After several Babylonian invasions (605, 597), Jerusalem and the First Temple are destroyed in 586 BCE. The Davidic monarchy ends; elites are deported to Babylon. Lamentations records the trauma.

quote.text: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion.

moments.takeaway: The Exile reshaped Judaism. Without Temple sacrifice possible, prayer, Torah study and synagogue worship developed in importance.

moments.title: Cyrus's return decree
moments.body: Cyrus conquers Babylon and allows exiles to return. The Second Temple is built (completed 516 BCE) under Zerubbabel and Joshua the High Priest. Many Jews remain in Babylon, founding the diaspora tradition.
moments.takeaway: Cyrus is called 'messiah' (anointed one) in Isaiah 45 — a striking application to a non-Jewish king.

moments.title: Ezra and Nehemiah
moments.body: Ezra brings the Torah from Babylon and reads it publicly in Jerusalem; Nehemiah rebuilds Jerusalem's walls. Strict reforms on mixed marriages and ritual purity. The biblical canon begins to take its final form.
moments.takeaway: Second Temple Judaism (516 BCE - 70 CE) saw the development of Pharisaic, Sadducean, Essene and (eventually) Christian movements.

now.title: Exile as paradigm
now.body: The exile-and-return pattern shapes Jewish identity. The 70 CE destruction of the Second Temple by Rome reset the framework into the rabbinic period. The 1948 founding of Israel is read by many as another return; the diaspora communities continue to flourish.
now.open_questions: How much of the Hebrew Bible took final form during or after the Exile? Mainstream scholarship sees major editorial work in the 6th-5th centuries BCE — the Documentary Hypothesis and its successors.

items.reflection: The Babylonian Exile transformed ancient Israelite religion into the prototype of modern Judaism — portable, text-centred, community-organised. The historical catastrophe became the theological foundation.

moments.title: Destruction of the Second Temple
moments.body: Temple destroyed 9 Av 70 CE. The traditional story: Yochanan ben Zakkai escapes Jerusalem in a coffin and persuades Vespasian to give him Yavneh (Jamnia) as a centre of Torah study. Rabbinic Judaism is born.
moments.takeaway: Without Temple sacrifice possible, the rabbinic project of preserving and elaborating Torah becomes Judaism's centre of gravity.

moments.title: Mishnah compiled
moments.body: Around 200 CE, Rabbi Judah the Prince compiles the Mishnah — the first written Oral Torah, in 63 tractates organised by topic. Hillel and Shammai's earlier schools, and the Tannaim of the first two centuries, are the basis.
moments.takeaway: The Mishnah was the first major Jewish text written after the Hebrew Bible. It remains a foundation of all subsequent rabbinic study.

moments.title: Talmuds completed
moments.body: The Mishnah generated commentary (Gemara) in both the Land of Israel and Babylonia. The Jerusalem Talmud is completed c. 400 CE; the Babylonian Talmud (longer, more authoritative) c. 500 CE. The Talmud's argumentative, dialectical style shapes Jewish learning for the next 1,500 years.

quote.text: These and these are the words of the living God.
quote.attrib: Eruvin 13b, on Hillel and Shammai's disputes

moments.takeaway: The Talmud is not a code but a record of argument. Multiple opinions coexist; the legal conclusion is one strand.

now.title: Living tradition
now.body: The Daf Yomi cycle (since 1923) takes participants through the entire Babylonian Talmud at one folio per day — 7.5 years per cycle. Hundreds of thousands now participate worldwide. Maimonides (Mishneh Torah, 1180), Joseph Karo (Shulchan Aruch, 1565) and Adin Steinsaltz (modern translation, 1965-2010) made the corpus more accessible to successive generations.
now.open_questions: How does rabbinic tradition handle modernity? Reform, Conservative and Orthodox movements have given different answers since the 19th century. The dialogue continues.

items.reflection: Rabbinic Judaism is one of the most successful textual cultures in history. A 1,500-year-old library is still studied daily, with new commentaries added in every generation. The Talmud's argumentative form makes the past present.

moments.title: Maimonides
moments.body: Born Cordoba (then under Almohad rule); family flees to Fez, then to Egypt. Court physician to Saladin's vizier. Codifies Jewish law, writes the Guide for the Perplexed (1190), produces Mishneh Torah (1180) — the first comprehensive code of Jewish law.
moments.takeaway: Maimonides combined Aristotelian philosophy with halakhic mastery. His 13 Principles of Faith remain a standard Jewish creedal statement.

moments.title: Mishneh Torah
moments.body: Maimonides completes the Mishneh Torah ('Second Torah'), 14 books organising all Jewish law systematically in clear Hebrew, without citation. Designed to make law accessible without years of Talmudic training.
moments.takeaway: The work was controversial — opponents felt it bypassed the Talmudic chain of reasoning. It became foundational.

moments.title: Guide for the Perplexed
moments.body: The Guide reconciles Judaism with Aristotelian philosophy, addressing the perplexed (the philosophically educated who struggle with biblical anthropomorphism). Translated into Hebrew (Ibn Tibbon, 1204) and Latin, it influences Aquinas and Christian scholasticism.

quote.text: From Moses to Moses, there was none like Moses.

moments.takeaway: Maimonides was buried at Tiberias; his tomb remains a major pilgrimage site.

now.title: Rambam in modern thought
now.body: Maimonides is foundational to Orthodox theology, Conservative scholarship, modern Jewish philosophy and Catholic philosophy (he influenced Aquinas). His medical writings have also drawn attention. Yeshiva University and others run continuous Maimonides studies.
now.open_questions: How rationalist was Maimonides? His esoteric writing (Leo Strauss read the Guide as concealing radical positions) and his more conventional halakhic works present different faces. Scholarship continues to debate.

items.reflection: A single Jewish thinker, working in Cairo under Muslim rule, codified Jewish law and reconciled it with Greek philosophy. His framework shaped not only Judaism but Christian theology and Islamic philosophy for the next 800 years.

moments.title: Baal Shem Tov
moments.body: Israel ben Eliezer (c. 1700-1760) — the Baal Shem Tov, 'master of the good name' — gathers followers in Podolia (now Ukraine). Teaches that joy, sincere prayer and devekut (cleaving to God) are accessible to ordinary Jews, not just learned scholars.
moments.takeaway: Hasidism emerged in a region of intense poverty and trauma (Khmelnytsky massacres 1648-49, ongoing antisemitic violence). Spiritual democratisation responded to scholarly elitism.

moments.title: Excommunication by the Vilna Gaon
moments.who: Elijah of Vilna (Vilna Gaon) and Mitnagdim
moments.body: The Vilna Gaon — the leading Talmudic scholar of his generation — declares Hasidism heretical (1772). Decades of bitter conflict between Hasidim and Mitnagdim (opponents) follow. Hasidism nevertheless grew rapidly.
moments.takeaway: By the early 19th century perhaps half of Eastern European Jews were Hasidic. Major dynasties (Belz, Satmar, Lubavitch/Chabad, Breslov, Ger) develop their own characters.

moments.title: Holocaust devastation
moments.body: Eastern European Hasidism was nearly annihilated in the Holocaust. The Lubavitcher Rebbe (Yosef Yitzchak Schneersohn, then Menachem Mendel Schneerson) rebuilds Chabad from Brooklyn. Satmar Hasidism rebuilds in Brooklyn and Israel.
moments.takeaway: Postwar Hasidism is a remarkable demographic recovery, with high birth rates and tight community organisation.

now.title: Living mysticism
now.body: Hasidic communities today number around 700,000-1 million worldwide, with major centres in Brooklyn, Jerusalem, Bnei Brak and London (Stamford Hill). Chabad's outreach extends to 100+ countries. Hasidic philosophy (Tanya, Sefat Emet, the Rebbe's talks) has influenced wider Jewish thought and broader spirituality (Martin Buber, Heschel).
now.open_questions: What is the relationship between Hasidism and modernity? Some movements (Chabad) engage extensively with the secular world; others (Satmar) define themselves by separation.

items.reflection: A spiritual movement born among 18th-century Polish villagers under impoverished conditions has become a major modern Jewish phenomenon. Hasidism's combination of joy, mysticism and community continues to attract followers in an increasingly secular world.

moments.title: Israel Jacobson opens Reform synagogue
moments.body: 1810: Israel Jacobson opens a Reform-style temple at Seesen with organ, German prayers, mixed seating, sermons. Reform Judaism is born in the German Haskalah (Jewish Enlightenment) — Mendelssohn's earlier translations and philosophy had prepared the ground.
moments.takeaway: Reform aimed to make Judaism compatible with modern German citizenship. Critics saw it as accommodation to assimilation.

moments.title: Pittsburgh Platform
moments.body: 1885: a conference of Reform rabbis at Pittsburgh issues the Platform — Judaism as 'progressive religion', dietary laws rejected, biblical scholarship welcomed, no return to Palestine sought, ethical mission central.
moments.takeaway: American Reform Judaism developed distinctively. Successive platforms (Columbus 1937, San Francisco 1976, Pittsburgh 1999) progressively re-embraced practices the 1885 Platform had abandoned.

moments.title: First female rabbi ordained
moments.body: 3 June 1972: Sally Priesand becomes the first female rabbi ordained in the US (and globally — Regina Jonas had been ordained privately in Germany 1935 and murdered in Auschwitz 1944). Conservative (1985), Reconstructionist and Modern Orthodox movements followed at different paces.
moments.takeaway: Gender equality is one of the major Jewish religious developments of the late 20th century — across most non-Orthodox movements.

now.title: Movements of modern Judaism
now.body: American Jewish population is split: about 35% Reform, 17% Conservative, 9% Orthodox, 4% Reconstructionist, the rest unaffiliated or other. Worldwide, Orthodoxy is proportionally larger. Reform Judaism (Progressive Judaism in the UK) is a global movement of around 1.8 million.
now.open_questions: Can Reform sustain itself with low fertility and high intermarriage? Orthodox communities are growing demographically; non-Orthodox movements are not. The future religious landscape may look different from the current one.

items.reflection: Modern Judaism is a family of responses to modernity. Reform, Conservative, Orthodox, Reconstructionist, Renewal and secular branches all emerged in the 19th-20th centuries as Jews navigated emancipation, modernity, persecution and statehood. The conversation continues.

moments.title: Wannsee Conference
moments.body: 20 January 1942: bureaucratisation of the Final Solution. The Holocaust kills around 6 million Jews — roughly two-thirds of European Jewry — between 1941 and 1945. Death camps (Auschwitz, Treblinka, Sobibor, Belzec, Chelmno), Einsatzgruppen shootings, ghetto starvation, transit and concentration camp deaths.
moments.takeaway: Reform, Orthodox, Hasidic, secular — every form of European Jewish life was targeted. The cultural loss is incalculable.

moments.title: Holocaust theology
moments.who: Richard Rubenstein, Emil Fackenheim, Eliezer Berkovits, Irving Greenberg
moments.body: Rubenstein's 'After Auschwitz' (1966) argues for the death of the God of history. Fackenheim formulates the '614th commandment': do not give Hitler posthumous victories. Berkovits defends classical theodicies. Greenberg's 'voluntary covenant' framework reshapes post-Holocaust Judaism.
moments.takeaway: Christian theology too was reshaped: Vatican II's Nostra Aetate (1965), Pope John Paul II's Yad Vashem visit (2000), the broader 'teaching of contempt' to 'teaching of respect' shift.

moments.title: Yad Vashem established
moments.body: Yad Vashem is established by Knesset law (1953) as Israel's official Holocaust memorial. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum opens in Washington (1993). Yom HaShoah (Holocaust Remembrance Day) was established in Israel 1959.
moments.takeaway: Survivor testimony, archival research and public commemoration became central to post-1945 Jewish identity worldwide.

now.title: Memory and presence
now.body: Last survivors are now in their late 90s. The transition to history-without-direct-witnesses is happening. Holocaust denial remains a criminal offence in many European countries. Modern educational programmes (Yad Vashem, USC Shoah Foundation, IWM) attempt to keep memory active. Contemporary antisemitism has risen sharply since 2015.
now.open_questions: Is the Holocaust unique or comparable? The historians' debate of the 1980s (Historikerstreit) raised the question; serious scholarship (Snyder, Friedländer) recognises both specificity and connection to other 20th-century atrocities.

items.reflection: The Holocaust is the defining event of 20th-century Jewish history and one of the most studied events in human history. Its theological, historical and political implications continue to shape Jewish thought and Christian-Jewish relations.

moments.title: Birth of Muhammad
moments.body: Muhammad ibn Abdullah, of the Quraysh tribe, is born in Mecca around 570 CE. Orphaned young, raised by his uncle Abu Talib. Marries Khadija (a wealthy widow) at 25; she is the first to believe in his prophethood at 40.
moments.takeaway: Khadija's role is central — first Muslim, first believer, financial supporter of the early community. Her death in 619 was a major personal loss.

moments.title: First revelation
moments.who: Muhammad in the Cave of Hira
moments.body: c. 610: at age 40, Muhammad receives the first revelation through Gabriel (Jibril) on Mount Hira outside Mecca. 'Iqra' ('Recite'). Public preaching begins around 613. The Meccan period is one of revelation, persecution and gradual community formation.
moments.takeaway: Muhammad's claim is to be the final prophet in the line of Abraham, Moses, Jesus. The Quran is delivered piecemeal over 23 years.

moments.title: Hijra to Medina
moments.body: 16 July 622 (revised): Muhammad and his followers emigrate from Mecca to Medina, fleeing persecution. The Constitution of Medina sets up the umma (community) including Muslims, Jews and pagans. The Islamic calendar dates from this year (AH 1).
moments.takeaway: The Hijra is the foundational political event of Islam, not the first revelation. Muslims date their calendar from the moment Islam became a community, not from a private religious experience.

moments.title: Death of Muhammad
moments.body: 8 June 632: Muhammad dies in Medina, in the house of Aisha. By then he had returned to Mecca (630), cleansed the Kaaba of idols, and most of Arabia had submitted. The succession crisis followed within hours.
moments.takeaway: The Sunni-Shia split has its origin in the succession dispute. The early Muslim community was politically as well as religiously coherent under Muhammad.

now.title: Islam today
now.body: Islam now has around 1.9 billion adherents — second largest world religion. The five pillars (shahada, salah, zakat, sawm, hajj), Quran (uniquely preserved in original Arabic), hadith collections, and four Sunni legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali) plus Shia jurisprudence shape practice.
now.open_questions: How accessible is the historical Muhammad? Islamic and Western academic sources differ in approach. Patricia Crone, Fred Donner and others have produced critical histories; the traditional biographical accounts (Sira) remain primary for Muslim communities.

items.reflection: A merchant in 7th-century Arabia experienced revelations that became the basis of the world's second-largest religion. The combination of religious teaching, political organisation and rapid territorial expansion produced a civilisation that reshaped Eurasia within a century.

moments.title: Revelation period
moments.body: The Quran is revealed to Muhammad over 23 years — Meccan (shorter, more poetic, theological) and Medinan (longer, more legal) verses. Memorisation by huffaz and partial recording on bones, parchment, leaves preserve the text during Muhammad's lifetime.
moments.takeaway: Oral transmission was the primary form of preservation. Even today, complete memorisation of the Quran (becoming a hafiz) is a major Muslim religious achievement.

moments.title: Abu Bakr's collection
moments.who: Abu Bakr, Umar, Zayd ibn Thabit
moments.body: After many huffaz die at the Battle of Yamama (633), Umar urges collection of the Quran. Abu Bakr commissions Zayd ibn Thabit (Muhammad's scribe) to compile a written text. This codex is given to Hafsa, Muhammad's widow, for safekeeping.
moments.takeaway: The threat of losing the text to oral transmission's mortality was the immediate trigger for codification.

moments.title: Uthmanic recension
moments.body: Around 650 CE, as different recitation variants emerged in different provinces, Uthman commissions a standard text based on Hafsa's codex. Copies are sent to major cities; variant codices are ordered destroyed. The Uthmanic text remains the basis of all modern Qurans.
moments.takeaway: The Sana'a manuscripts (discovered 1972) and Birmingham fragment (dated 568-645 by carbon, 2015) confirm extremely early dating of substantial parts of the text.

now.title: Living recitation
now.body: Quranic recitation (tajwid) follows precise rules of pronunciation and rhythm. Major competitions and the international Quran competition draw participants from across the Muslim world. Tafsir (Quranic commentary) — al-Tabari (10th c.), al-Razi (12th c.), Ibn Kathir (14th c.) — continues to be produced; contemporary commentaries engage with modern questions.
now.open_questions: When exactly was the canonical text fixed? Most Western scholarship now broadly accepts the traditional dating of around 650 CE for substantive completion. Earlier Crone-Wansbrough hyper-revisionism has lost ground.

items.reflection: The Quran is preserved in a uniquely consistent way among major scriptures — one canonical text in one language for 1,400 years. The combination of oral and written transmission produced a stability without parallel in comparable religious traditions.

moments.title: Conquest of Iberia
moments.body: 711: Tariq ibn Ziyad crosses from Morocco at Gibraltar (Jebel Tariq). Visigothic Spain collapses within years. The peninsula becomes al-Andalus. Cordoba is established as capital of the Umayyad emirate (then caliphate from 929).
moments.takeaway: Within a generation, Muslim rule extended from the Indus to the Pyrenees. The Pyrenees stopped only after the Battle of Tours/Poitiers (732).

moments.title: Cordoba golden age
moments.who: Abd al-Rahman III and the Caliphate
moments.body: Cordoba is one of the world's great cities — perhaps 400,000-500,000 people, library of 400,000 volumes, street lighting, paved streets. Jewish, Christian and Muslim scholars exchange learning. Hasdai ibn Shaprut, Maimonides's predecessors, the philosopher al-Farabi all flourish.
moments.takeaway: 'Convivencia' (coexistence) is a contested term — there was significant intercommunal dialogue but also dhimmi restrictions and periodic violence. The history was neither golden nor genocidal.

moments.title: Granada falls
moments.body: 2 January 1492: Granada surrenders, ending Muslim rule in Iberia. The Alhambra Decree (31 March 1492) expels Jews. The 1499 Mudejar revolt is followed by forced conversion of Muslims. The Inquisition targets converts.
moments.takeaway: 1492 closes the Andalusian chapter and opens others — Columbus sails the same year. The Sephardic diaspora settles across the Mediterranean and beyond.

now.title: Reading al-Andalus
now.body: The 'convivencia' debate runs between Maria Rosa Menocal's 'Ornament of the World' (2002) and more critical historians (Dario Fernandez-Morera). Modern Muslims and Jews have idealised aspects; modern Christians have selectively forgotten the Reconquista violence. The Alhambra, Cordoba mosque-cathedral, and Sephardic communities remain.
now.open_questions: How tolerant was al-Andalus? More than contemporaneous Christian Europe; less than 20th-century idealisations. The reality varied by period, region and ruler.

items.reflection: Islamic Spain produced one of the great civilisational syntheses — Arab, Berber, Visigothic, Jewish, Christian. The 1492 closure reset European religious geography. The cultural inheritance — in architecture, language, music, food — still permeates Iberia.

moments.title: Constantinople falls
moments.body: 29 May 1453: Mehmed II ('the Conqueror') captures Constantinople after a 53-day siege. Hagia Sophia is converted to a mosque. Constantinople becomes Istanbul, capital of the Ottoman Empire. The Byzantine Empire ends after 1,123 years.
moments.takeaway: The fall closes the medieval period in Eastern Europe and confirms Ottoman power across the eastern Mediterranean.

moments.title: Caliphate transfers
moments.body: 1517: Selim I defeats the Mamluks and conquers Egypt, Syria, the Hijaz. The Abbasid caliph in Cairo transfers the title to the Ottoman Sultan. Mecca and Medina now under Ottoman protection. Selim takes the title 'Servant of the Two Holy Places'.
moments.takeaway: The Ottoman Sultan is now also Caliph — the formal head of Sunni Islam. The role lasts until 1924.

moments.title: Caliphate abolished
moments.body: 3 March 1924: the Caliphate is abolished by Kemal Atatürk's secular Turkish state. The last Ottoman Caliph Abdülmecid II is exiled. For the first time since the death of Muhammad, there is no caliph.
moments.takeaway: The absence of an institutional caliphate has shaped 20th-21st century Islamist movements. ISIS's 2014 claim to restoration of the caliphate was a particular distorted form.

now.title: Post-caliphate Islam
now.body: Most contemporary Muslims see the formal caliphate as historically closed. Modern Islamist movements (Muslim Brotherhood, Hizb ut-Tahrir) have wanted to restore it; mainstream scholarship in major Sunni institutions (al-Azhar) has not endorsed this. The Hagia Sophia was reconverted to a mosque in 2020.
now.open_questions: Is a caliphate possible in the modern state system? Practical implementation faces national sovereignty obstacles. Symbolically, the longing for unified Muslim political community remains powerful.

items.reflection: For 1,300 years after Muhammad, Sunni Islam had an institutional head, even when nominal. The 1924 abolition opened a space in which different movements have competed to claim authority. The political geography of contemporary Islam still reflects that unresolved question.

moments.title: Asoka's reign
moments.body: Asoka ruled the Mauryan empire — almost all of the Indian subcontinent. After the conquest of Kalinga (c. 261 BCE), with around 100,000 deaths, he converted to Buddhism. He proclaimed his commitment through inscriptions across the empire.
moments.takeaway: Asoka's Rock and Pillar Edicts (the earliest substantial Indian writing in Brahmi script) are some of the most important Buddhist textual evidence.

moments.title: Buddhist missions
moments.body: Asoka sponsors Buddhist missions: to Sri Lanka (Mahinda), to South-East Asia, to Hellenistic kingdoms (Antiochus II, Ptolemy II). Sri Lankan Theravada Buddhism dates from this mission. Asoka also calls the Third Buddhist Council (probably c. 250 BCE) at Pataliputra.
moments.takeaway: Buddhism's global spread began as imperial sponsorship. From this network, missions to China (1st c. CE), Korea, Japan (6th c.), Tibet (7th c.) followed.

moments.title: Sanchi stupa begun
moments.body: Asoka commissioned major Buddhist monuments including the Great Stupa at Sanchi. The lion capital of Asoka's pillar at Sarnath later became India's state emblem (1950).
moments.takeaway: Asoka's symbols outlived the Mauryan empire by two millennia and were chosen by independent India for its national identity.

now.title: Asoka in modern India
now.body: Asoka's chakra (wheel of dharma) is at the centre of the Indian flag. His pillars and edicts are major archaeological monuments. Buddhist revival in India (Ambedkar's mass conversion 1956, Tibetan diaspora 1959) has restored a tradition that had largely faded from its homeland.
now.open_questions: How sincere was Asoka's conversion? The edicts present a developed philosophy of governance through dharma; critics suggest political consolidation. Most historians treat the religious shift as substantial.

items.reflection: A 3rd-century BCE Indian emperor's conversion shaped the spread of one of the world's great religions. The Asokan template — religious patronage as imperial policy — would be repeated by Constantine, Charlemagne, the Tang emperors and others. State-sponsored religion is a recurrent pattern in world history.

moments.title: Composition
moments.body: The Bhagavad Gita ('Song of the Lord') is 700 verses, embedded in the Mahabharata (Book 6, Bhishma Parva). On the eve of battle, Arjuna refuses to fight his kinsmen; his charioteer Krishna reveals himself as the supreme God and teaches Arjuna about dharma (duty), the paths of yoga, and the eternal self.
moments.takeaway: The Gita synthesises bhakti (devotion), jnana (knowledge) and karma (action) yogas. It has been read for two millennia as a self-contained spiritual classic.

moments.title: Shankara's commentary
moments.body: Shankara's commentary on the Gita is the most influential of many. He reads the text as supporting Advaita (non-dualist) Vedanta. Later commentators (Ramanuja, qualified non-dualism; Madhva, dualist) offer different theological readings.
moments.takeaway: The Gita is a major site of Hindu theological debate — its capaciousness allows multiple schools to claim it.

moments.title: Gandhi's reading
moments.body: Gandhi read the Gita as a constant guide. His commentary 'The Gita according to Gandhi' (1929-32) reads the battle as a metaphor for the inner moral struggle. Bhakti and ahimsa (non-violence) are reconciled.

quote.text: When doubts haunt me, when disappointments stare me in the face, I open the Bhagavad Gita and find a verse to comfort me.

moments.takeaway: Gandhi's selective reading was politically powerful but theologically contested. Earlier nationalist readings (Bal Gangadhar Tilak) treated the text as calling for action even violent.

now.title: Global text
now.body: The Gita has been translated into all major world languages — Wilkins 1785 was the first English version; Emerson read it; Oppenheimer quoted it at Trinity. Modern global yoga and Hindu diaspora communities draw on the text. ISKCON (Hare Krishna) uses Prabhupada's translation.
now.open_questions: Is the Gita pacifist or activist? Different readings have supported colonial-era violence, Gandhi's non-violence, and contemporary Hindu nationalism. The text's openness allows competing applications.

items.reflection: A 2,000-year-old dialogue on a battlefield has become a defining text of Hindu philosophy and global spirituality. Its multiple yogic paths, its theology of devotion, and its meditation on duty have spoken to readers in radically different historical contexts.

moments.title: Parliament of the World's Religions
moments.body: 11 September 1893: Swami Vivekananda (Narendranath Datta), 30 years old, addresses the Parliament of Religions in Chicago. 'Sisters and brothers of America.' His Neo-Vedanta presentation of Hinduism as universal, tolerant and philosophical caused a sensation.

quote.text: I am proud to belong to a religion which has taught the world both tolerance and universal acceptance.
quote.attrib: Swami Vivekananda, Parliament of Religions, 11 September 1893

moments.takeaway: Vivekananda's framing of Hinduism for a Western audience — universal, rational, mystical — shaped Western perceptions for generations.

moments.title: Lectures across America and Europe
moments.body: Vivekananda lectures across the US (Detroit, Chicago, Boston, New York), establishes Vedanta Societies (San Francisco 1900 still active), travels to England. Returns to India 1897 to found the Ramakrishna Mission.
moments.takeaway: Modern global yoga and meditation traditions trace partly to Vivekananda's late-19th-century outreach.

moments.title: Death
moments.body: 4 July 1902: Vivekananda dies aged 39 at Belur Math, near Calcutta. His complete works (around nine volumes) continue to be read. The Ramakrishna Mission and Math grew into a major Indian religious-philanthropic organisation.
moments.takeaway: Vivekananda's reframing of Hindu identity influenced Indian nationalism, the Indian Diaspora, and what Westerners think 'Hinduism' is.

now.title: Neo-Vedanta's reach
now.body: The Vedanta Societies, Self-Realisation Fellowship (Yogananda, 1920), Transcendental Meditation (Maharishi Mahesh Yogi, 1958), ISKCON (Prabhupada, 1965) and others extended the Hindu global presence. International Yoga Day (21 June, since 2014) institutionalised Indian soft power. Around 200 million practice some form of yoga globally.
now.open_questions: Is Neo-Vedanta authentically representative of Hinduism? Critics argue it homogenises a diverse tradition for Western consumption. Defenders argue it makes accessible what the tradition genuinely contains.

items.reflection: A single 1893 lecture began Hinduism's modern global presence. Vivekananda's combination of philosophical sophistication, mystical claim and universalist framing succeeded in making a tradition external audiences had viewed exotically seem accessible — and influential.

moments.title: Tegh Bahadur martyred
moments.body: 11 November 1675: Guru Tegh Bahadur is beheaded in Delhi by Aurangzeb's order, having refused to convert to Islam and having defended the religious freedom of Kashmiri Hindus. His severed head was carried to his son Gobind Rai.
moments.takeaway: The martyrdom shapes Sikh identity. The defence of religious freedom is foundational.

moments.title: Vaisakhi and the Khalsa
moments.body: Vaisakhi 1699: Guru Gobind Singh calls a great assembly. He asks for volunteers willing to die for the faith. Five men step forward in turn — Panj Pyare (Five Beloved Ones). They are initiated with amrit (sweetened water stirred with a double-edged sword); they then initiate the Guru himself.

quote.text: Wahe Guru Ji Ka Khalsa, Wahe Guru Ji Ki Fateh.

moments.takeaway: The Khalsa is marked by the Five Ks: kesh (uncut hair), kara (steel bracelet), kanga (comb), kachera (undershorts), kirpan (sword). Men take the surname Singh ('lion'), women Kaur ('princess').

moments.title: Guru Granth Sahib as eternal Guru
moments.body: October 1708: Guru Gobind Singh, before his death from a Mughal assassin's wound, declares the Guru Granth Sahib the eternal Guru. There will be no more human Gurus. The scripture, compiled by Guru Arjan with later additions, becomes the focus of Sikh worship.
moments.takeaway: Scripture-as-Guru ends the succession question. The Guru Granth Sahib is treated as a living Guru.

now.title: Khalsa identity
now.body: Vaisakhi is the major Sikh festival, marking the Khalsa's founding. The Five Ks are practised by initiated (Amritdhari) Sikhs; many practising Sikhs do not take amrit but observe Sikh values. The 1984 attack on the Golden Temple (Operation Blue Star) and subsequent Khalistan tensions still shape contemporary Sikh politics.
now.open_questions: What is the relationship between Khalsa identity and Sikh identity more broadly? The question shapes contemporary debates about who counts as a Sikh in political and religious senses.

items.reflection: The Khalsa transformed Sikhism into a distinct religious community with a clear collective identity. The combination of spiritual discipline, social equality (equal surnames, langar, anti-caste teaching) and martial readiness has shaped the tradition for 300 years.

moments.title: Punjab insurgency
moments.body: Sant Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale leads a militant Sikh political-religious movement based at the Golden Temple, Amritsar. Demands include greater Punjab autonomy and ultimately the independent state of Khalistan. Violence escalates 1981-84.
moments.takeaway: Bhindranwale's relationship with Khalistan was complex; he was sometimes ambiguous about formal independence but increasingly militant about Sikh identity.

moments.title: Operation Blue Star
moments.who: Indian Army at the Golden Temple complex
moments.body: 1-8 June 1984: the Indian Army storms the Golden Temple complex. Tanks enter Harmandir Sahib (the central shrine). Bhindranwale killed. Estimated deaths: 500-2,000+ depending on source. The Akal Takht (one of the most sacred Sikh structures) is heavily damaged.
moments.takeaway: The attack on the Golden Temple on a major Sikh holy day (martyrdom day of Guru Arjan) traumatised Sikhs globally.

moments.title: Indira Gandhi assassinated
moments.who: Beant Singh and Satwant Singh, Indira's Sikh bodyguards
moments.body: 31 October 1984: Indira Gandhi is shot by her Sikh bodyguards at her Delhi residence. In the following days, anti-Sikh pogroms across Delhi and elsewhere kill around 3,000 Sikhs in officially counted figures (probably higher in reality). Many of the violence's instigators were Congress Party members; convictions have been few.
moments.takeaway: The 1984 sequence — Blue Star, assassination, pogroms — is foundational trauma for modern Sikhism. The Indian government's failure to prosecute pogrom organisers remains contested.

now.title: Memory and ongoing politics
now.body: The Akal Takht was rebuilt and the Golden Temple complex restored. Khalistan as movement has weakened but persists in parts of the diaspora. Recent diplomatic tensions (Canada-India 2023 over the killing of a Khalistani activist) extend the story.
now.open_questions: How should the Indian state apologise for 1984? Various commissions (Mishra, Nanavati, others) have produced incomplete acknowledgements. The pogrom convictions are still being pursued by some families and the Sikh community.

items.reflection: A military operation on a sacred site, a political assassination, and a state-tolerated pogrom — the 1984 sequence remains an unhealed wound in modern Sikh consciousness. The political and religious dimensions cannot be separated.

moments.title: Proslogion
moments.body: 1077-78: Anselm of Canterbury writes the Proslogion. Chapter 2 contains the ontological argument: God is 'that than which nothing greater can be thought'. If God existed only in the mind, a greater being (one existing also in reality) could be thought — so God must exist in reality.

quote.text: Aliquid quo nihil maius cogitari possit.

moments.takeaway: The argument moves from definition to existence — uniquely controversial among arguments for God. Most theistic arguments use experience or causation; Anselm uses pure concept.

moments.title: Gaunilo's criticism
moments.body: Gaunilo, a fellow Benedictine monk, replies with the 'perfect island' parody: by the same logic, the perfect island must exist. Anselm responds: the argument applies only to a maximally great being, not to contingent things.
moments.takeaway: The argument has been continuously debated. Aquinas rejected it; Descartes (Meditations, 1641) revived it; Hume and Kant criticised it (existence is not a predicate, Kant 1781).

moments.title: Plantinga's modal version
moments.body: Norman Malcolm (1960) and Alvin Plantinga (1974, 'The Nature of Necessity') develop modal versions of the argument using possible-worlds semantics. If a maximally great being is possible (exists in some possible world), then by definition of maximal greatness it exists in all possible worlds — including the actual.
moments.takeaway: Modern modal logic gave the ontological argument a technical apparatus Anselm didn't have. Its persuasiveness still depends on the premise of possibility.

now.title: An argument that won't die
now.body: The ontological argument remains philosophically alive — Graham Oppy's surveys, William Lane Craig's lectures, Plantinga's continuing work. Few are converted by it; many find it interesting. It is on A-level Religious Studies syllabuses.
now.open_questions: Does existence follow from concept? Kant's critique (existence is not a predicate) is the standard response. Plantinga's modal version sidesteps but doesn't refute Kant's point.

items.reflection: A short chapter in an 11th-century devotional text generated a philosophical argument debated continuously for nearly 1,000 years.
