The ontological argument may not convince anyone of God's existence, but it has driven serious work in logic, modal metaphysics and the philosophy of language.

moments.title: Of Miracles
moments.who: David Hume, Enquiry concerning Human Understanding
moments.body: Section X of the Enquiry (1748) argues that no testimony to a miracle can ever justify belief. The wise calibrate belief to evidence; testimony to violation of laws of nature is always less probable than the testimony's falseness or mistake.
moments.takeaway: Hume's miracles argument has been continuously debated. Modern Bayesian formulations (Earman 'Hume's Abject Failure', 2000) attempt to either rescue or refute it.

moments.title: Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
moments.body: Hume wrote the Dialogues over decades; they were published posthumously (1779). Three characters — Demea (orthodox), Cleanthes (natural theologian, design argument), Philo (sceptic, often Hume's voice) — debate. The design argument is subjected to its most thorough early criticism.

quote.text: What peculiar privilege has this little agitation of the brain which we call thought, that we must thus make it the model of the whole universe?

moments.takeaway: Hume's design critique anticipates Darwin (who provided the alternative mechanism). The problem of evil also takes its modern form in the Dialogues.

moments.title: Hume's death
moments.who: Adam Smith and the Edinburgh circle
moments.body: August 1776: Hume dies in Edinburgh. Adam Smith's letter to William Strahan describes Hume's death — calm, sceptical, refusing the deathbed conversion expected of unbelievers. The letter caused outrage in religious circles.
moments.takeaway: Hume's serene death was as much a public argument as his books — a model of philosophical equanimity without religious consolation.

now.title: Hume's lasting influence
now.body: Hume is the canonical philosopher of religious scepticism. Modern atheism (Dennett, Dawkins) draws on his arguments; modern theistic responses (Plantinga, Swinburne) engage them. The Dialogues remain on philosophy of religion syllabuses worldwide.
now.open_questions: Was Hume an atheist or a deist? Almost certainly an atheist or close to it. His public caution reflected his time; his private letters and posthumous works clarify his views.

items.reflection: The Scottish Enlightenment's leading philosopher subjected natural religion to systematic critique. Hume's arguments — about miracles, design, the problem of evil — remain the framework in which modern philosophy of religion operates.

moments.title: Critique of Pure Reason
moments.body: Kant's first Critique distinguishes phenomena (the world as we experience it) from noumena (the world as it is in itself). Pure reason cannot prove God's existence — the ontological, cosmological and teleological arguments all fail. But practical reason (ethics) may require God as postulate.
moments.takeaway: Kant's 'I have therefore found it necessary to deny knowledge, in order to make room for faith' (1787 second edition preface) became a touchstone for liberal theology.

moments.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
moments.body: Kant's Groundwork formulates the categorical imperative. Formula of Universal Law: act only on that maxim by which you can at the same time will that it become a universal law. Formula of Humanity: act so that you treat humanity, whether in your own person or in that of another, always as an end and never merely as a means.

quote.text: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe... the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.

moments.takeaway: Deontological ethics — duty-based rather than consequence-based — is a Kantian inheritance. Most modern human-rights frameworks owe more to Kant than to Bentham.

moments.title: Religion within the Boundaries of Mere Reason
moments.body: Kant treats religion as rational moral commitment with historical elements as vehicle. Original sin is reinterpreted as the propensity to evil in human nature. Salvation is moral transformation. The book brought Prussian censorship; Kant agreed not to publish on religion until Frederick William II's death (1797).
moments.takeaway: Kant's philosophical religion — moral, autonomous, rational — shaped 19th-century liberal Protestantism.

now.title: Kant in modern ethics
now.body: Deontological ethics dominates one major strand of philosophy of religion and moral philosophy. Christine Korsgaard, Onora O'Neill, Allen Wood and others have produced major modern Kantian programmes. The categorical imperative remains a staple of A-level ethics.
now.open_questions: Can a purely rational ethics be religiously satisfactory? Kant thought yes; orthodox theology has often thought no. The dialogue continues in modern Christian and Jewish ethics.

items.reflection: A Königsberg philosopher who never travelled more than 100 km from his home reshaped Western moral philosophy. Kant's combination of rational duty, autonomous individual and universalisable moral law is foundational to modern ethics, human rights, and one form of philosophical religion.

moments.title: Gifford Lectures
moments.body: 1901-02: William James delivers the Gifford Lectures at Edinburgh. Published as 'The Varieties of Religious Experience' (1902). The lectures treat religious experience phenomenologically — what is the structure of conversion, mysticism, sainthood, prayer — rather than as theological doctrine.
moments.takeaway: James's pragmatist approach: religious experiences are real psychological phenomena; their cognitive content is to be tested by their fruits ('by their fruits ye shall know them').

moments.title: Four marks of mystical experience
moments.body: James identifies four marks of mystical experience: ineffability (cannot be adequately described), noetic quality (knowledge-yielding), transiency (brief), and passivity (received, not generated). These four marks shape subsequent academic study of mysticism.

quote.text: Religion shall mean for us the feelings, acts, and experiences of individual men in their solitude, so far as they apprehend themselves to stand in relation to whatever they may consider the divine.
quote.attrib: William James, Varieties of Religious Experience, 1902

moments.takeaway: James separated personal religion from institutional religion. His focus on the former shaped modern study of spirituality.

moments.title: Pragmatism
moments.body: James's 'Pragmatism' (1907) treats religious beliefs as practical hypotheses. A belief's truth is its workability — whether holding it produces good outcomes for the believer. 'The will to believe' (1896) had defended the right to believe under conditions of evidential uncertainty.
moments.takeaway: Pragmatism opened space for religious belief that wasn't rationally compelled but wasn't irrational. This has remained a major framework in liberal religious thought.

now.title: Empirical study of religion
now.body: James founded the empirical psychology of religion. Modern neuroscience of religious experience (Andrew Newberg, Mario Beauregard), survey research (Pew Research Religion), and cognitive science of religion (Pascal Boyer, Justin Barrett) extend the programme. The Varieties remains continuously in print.
now.open_questions: Are religious experiences evidential? James thought they couldn't establish doctrine but supported the right to believe. Modern philosophers (William Alston, Alvin Plantinga) have developed proper-basicality arguments going further.

items.reflection: An American psychologist turned the study of religion from doctrinal to experiential. James's framework — religious experience as phenomenon to be studied empirically — opened a century of work in psychology, sociology and philosophy of religion.

moments.title: Bentham's Introduction
moments.body: Bentham publishes 'An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation' (1789). The principle of utility: actions are right insofar as they promote happiness, wrong as they produce its reverse. The 'felicific calculus' attempts to measure pleasure and pain.

quote.text: The greatest happiness of the greatest number is the foundation of morals and legislation.
quote.attrib: Bentham, attributed (the principle is in his work; the exact phrasing was Hutcheson's)

moments.takeaway: Bentham's project: reform English law along rational utilitarian lines. The 1832 Reform Act and many subsequent reforms had utilitarian intellectual basis.

moments.title: Mill's Utilitarianism
moments.body: Mill's essays 'Utilitarianism' (Fraser's Magazine, 1861; book 1863) refine Bentham's framework. Mill distinguishes higher and lower pleasures ('better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied'). Defends utilitarianism against the charge of swine philosophy.
moments.takeaway: Mill makes utilitarianism less reductive and more humanistic. Higher pleasures (intellect, art, friendship) outweigh lower pleasures (sensory) in his calculus.

moments.title: Modern utilitarianism
moments.body: Singer's 'Animal Liberation' (1975) extends utilitarianism to non-human animals. Effective Altruism (since 2009 William MacAskill, Peter Singer, Toby Ord) applies utilitarian reasoning to charity. Critics (Bernard Williams, John Rawls) have developed alternatives.
moments.takeaway: Utilitarianism remains one of the two main ethical frameworks alongside deontology. Most public policy reasoning is implicitly utilitarian.

now.title: Utilitarianism today
now.body: Modern variants include act/rule utilitarianism, preference utilitarianism (Singer), negative utilitarianism (minimise suffering), and global utilitarianism (Parfit, Bostrom). The framework's strengths (decisiveness, comparability) and weaknesses (rights, fairness, distributive concerns) are continuously debated.
now.open_questions: How should utility be measured and across whom? Hedonistic vs preference vs objective-list theories of welfare; aggregation across individuals; treatment of future generations all remain contested.

items.reflection: Two English philosophers built the framework most modern public policy uses implicitly. Cost-benefit analysis, QALY-based healthcare resource allocation, animal welfare regulation all bear utilitarian fingerprints. The framework's limits — when utility conflicts with rights — remain live in every public ethics debate.

moments.title: Situation Ethics published
moments.body: 1966: Fletcher publishes 'Situation Ethics: The New Morality'. The principle: the only intrinsic good is love (agape). Rules are guides, not absolutes; the loving thing to do depends on the situation. Six fundamental propositions.
moments.takeaway: Fletcher's work fitted the 1960s — second-wave feminism, sexual revolution, civil rights, Vatican II. It was widely read and widely condemned.

moments.title: Six propositions
moments.body: Fletcher's six fundamental propositions: 1. Only love is intrinsically good. 2. The ruling norm of decision is love. 3. Love and justice are the same. 4. Love wills the neighbour's good, whether we like him or not. 5. Only the end justifies the means. 6. Decisions ought to be made situationally, not prescriptively.
moments.takeaway: Critics: a charter for antinomianism (rejection of moral law). Defenders: a recovery of the Pauline ethic of love.

moments.title: Humanae Vitae as counter
moments.body: 25 July 1968: Pope Paul VI's encyclical 'Humanae Vitae' reaffirms Catholic teaching against artificial contraception. The encyclical can be read as a counter-statement to the situational ethics that had become prominent. Many Catholic theologians and laypeople disagree.
moments.takeaway: The 1968 reaffirmation of natural law against situationism shaped post-Vatican-II Catholic moral theology.

now.title: Situational versus principled
now.body: Situation Ethics remains on A-level Religious Studies syllabuses. Few contemporary academic ethicists are pure situationists, but proportionalism, virtue ethics with practical wisdom, and care ethics all share Fletcher's resistance to mechanical rule-application.
now.open_questions: How can we know what love demands? Critics argue situationism collapses into moral relativism without principles to guide judgement. Defenders argue moral judgement always requires situational wisdom — Aristotle's phronesis.

items.reflection: A 1960s Episcopal theologian provoked one of the most lasting Christian ethical debates. The question — how do general principles (love, justice) connect to particular decisions? — remains central to Christian ethics.

moments.title: Nicomachean Ethics
moments.body: Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics treats ethics as a practical inquiry into the good life (eudaimonia). Moral virtues (courage, justice, temperance) are developed by habituation; intellectual virtues (practical wisdom, theoretical wisdom) by teaching. Virtues are means between extremes.
moments.takeaway: Aristotle's framework dominated Western ethics into the Middle Ages, was revived by Aquinas, and is the basis of modern virtue ethics.

moments.title: Aquinas adapts Aristotle
moments.body: Aquinas adopts Aristotle's framework for Catholic moral theology. The cardinal virtues (Aristotle's: prudence, justice, fortitude, temperance) and theological virtues (Paul's: faith, hope, love) form a complete system. Natural law derives partly from this.
moments.takeaway: Catholic moral theology continues to use Aristotelian-Thomist categories. Aristotle's influence in this tradition has been continuous for 800 years.

moments.title: Modern Virtue Ethics revived
moments.body: Anscombe's 'Modern Moral Philosophy' (Philosophy, 1958) argues that deontology and utilitarianism are both bankrupt without theological foundations and proposes returning to Aristotelian virtue ethics. Alasdair MacIntyre's 'After Virtue' (1981), Philippa Foot, Rosalind Hursthouse extend the project.
moments.takeaway: Virtue ethics is now one of the three main contemporary ethical frameworks alongside deontology and consequentialism.

now.title: Virtue ethics today
now.body: Modern virtue ethics is large and diverse — secular Aristotelians, Christian Thomists, care ethicists, feminist virtue theorists. Character education in schools, military ethics, medical ethics (Pellegrino's virtue-based medical ethics) draw on the tradition.
now.open_questions: Can virtue ethics provide action-guiding rules? Critics argue it can't tell us what to do in particular cases. Defenders argue this is exactly the point — ethical decisions require practical wisdom that algorithms can't replace.

items.reflection: A 4th-century BCE Greek philosopher's lectures on ethics have been continuously studied for nearly 2,400 years. Aristotle's combination of practical wisdom, virtue cultivation and human flourishing remains a major framework — and has had a notable modern revival.

moments.title: Aquinas develops natural law
moments.body: Aquinas's natural law: eternal law (God's reason) is reflected in natural law (the law of human nature) and codified by divine law (revelation) and human law (positive law). Primary precepts: preserve life, reproduce, educate young, live in society, know God.
moments.takeaway: Natural law is a Catholic synthesis of Aristotelian teleology and biblical theology. The Aristotelian view that things have natures and purposes (teloi) underpins the moral conclusions.

moments.title: Natural law in international thought
moments.body: Spanish School (Suarez), then Protestant thinkers (Grotius's 'On the Law of War and Peace', 1625), develop natural law into the basis of international law and human rights theory. The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man draws on natural-law assumptions.
moments.takeaway: Natural law was a major intellectual current of the 17th-18th centuries before being eclipsed by positivism and historicism in the 19th.

moments.title: Humanae Vitae and the contemporary debate
moments.body: 1968: Humanae Vitae's prohibition of artificial contraception is grounded in natural-law reasoning about the unitive and procreative aspects of sexual intercourse. Many lay Catholics and some theologians dissent. The natural-law framework is increasingly contested — and increasingly defended by 'new natural law' theorists (Finnis, Grisez, George).
moments.takeaway: Natural law continues to shape Catholic positions on contraception, abortion, euthanasia, marriage. New natural law theorists (John Finnis) defend it without the Aristotelian-Thomist metaphysics.

now.title: Natural law debated
now.body: Natural law is taught in every Catholic seminary. Outside Catholic moral theology, it is one option among many. Modern human rights discourse owes natural-law inheritance even when not acknowledged. Critics (Hume on is-ought, modern Darwinism on natures) have produced powerful objections.
now.open_questions: Does nature have purposes? The Aristotelian view that it does has been undermined by Darwinian biology in many readings. New natural lawyers (Finnis) defend the framework without Aristotelian biology by appeal to basic human goods.

items.reflection: Natural law is one of the longest-running ethical frameworks in Western thought. Its modern Catholic form is doctrinally fixed; its philosophical defenders continue to develop the framework; its critics are many. Few ethical traditions have lasted longer or generated more debate.

moments.title: Copernicus posthumous publication
moments.body: May 1543: 'De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium' published as Copernicus lies on his deathbed. The Sun, not the Earth, is the centre. The book includes a preface (by Andreas Osiander, without Copernicus's authority) presenting heliocentrism as a calculational hypothesis rather than physical truth.
moments.takeaway: The Copernican model was initially treated as a mathematical convenience by the church. Real trouble came when Galileo argued it was physically true.

moments.title: Sidereus Nuncius
moments.body: March 1610: Galileo publishes 'The Starry Messenger' describing telescope observations — mountains on the Moon, moons of Jupiter, phases of Venus. The phases of Venus are decisive evidence against the Ptolemaic model.
moments.takeaway: Galileo's observational evidence put the church in a position where the choice between Aristotelian-Ptolemaic and Copernican was scientific, not philosophical.

moments.title: Galileo's trial
moments.body: 22 June 1633: Galileo is condemned by the Inquisition for his 'Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems' (1632). He recants. House arrest until death (1642). The legend 'And yet it moves' (Eppur si muove) is later apocryphal.
moments.takeaway: Pope John Paul II in 1992 acknowledged that the church had erred in its treatment of Galileo. The reconciliation was 359 years coming.

now.title: Science and religion
now.body: The Galileo affair is the canonical case of religion-science conflict. Other examples (Darwin and creationism, contemporary debates over evolution in US schools, Vatican Observatory) extend or complicate it. The 'warfare' thesis (White, Draper, late 19th c.) has been substantially complicated by recent historians (Numbers, Brooke).
now.open_questions: Are religion and science fundamentally conflict-prone or compatible? Most contemporary historians (John Hedley Brooke 'Science and Religion', 1991) argue the relationship has been complex — sometimes conflict, often cooperation, mostly independence.

items.reflection: The Galileo case is more nuanced than popular narratives suggest. The church wasn't anti-science — it sponsored astronomy and natural philosophy — but it did claim authority over biblical interpretation and applied it to physical questions where it had no expertise. The lesson — that institutions overstep their competence — recurs.

moments.title: Voyage of the Beagle
moments.body: 1831-36: Darwin's five-year voyage on HMS Beagle. Galapagos finches, fossil mammals of South America, marine geology. The observations slowly congeal into the theory of natural selection by the late 1830s.
moments.takeaway: Darwin was preparing for the clergy when he joined the Beagle. The voyage gave him both data and a 20-year framework for synthesis.

moments.title: On the Origin of Species
moments.body: 24 November 1859: 'On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection' published. 1,250 copies sell on the first day. Darwin had delayed publication for 20 years; Alfred Russel Wallace's 1858 letter (with the same theory) forced the issue.

quote.text: There is grandeur in this view of life.
quote.attrib: Darwin, closing sentence of the Origin

moments.takeaway: The Origin treated humans only briefly. Darwin's 'Descent of Man' (1871) addressed human evolution directly.

moments.title: Oxford debate
moments.body: 30 June 1860: at the British Association meeting in Oxford, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce ('Soapy Sam') challenges T.H. Huxley ('Darwin's bulldog') about Darwin's theory. The exchange — including Wilberforce's apocryphal question about Huxley's monkey ancestry — became iconic of the science-religion conflict.
moments.takeaway: The actual debate was probably less dramatic than later accounts. But the symbolic moment captured the cultural collision.

now.title: Faith and evolution
now.body: Most Christian denominations (Catholic, mainline Protestant, most evangelical) accept evolution. Pope Pius XII's 'Humani Generis' (1950) permitted Catholic engagement with evolution; John Paul II (1996) affirmed it as 'more than just a hypothesis'. Young-Earth creationism (around 40% of US adults per Gallup) remains substantial but is a minority globally. Intelligent Design has had limited scientific success but continuing cultural presence.
now.open_questions: How is religious belief affected by evolution? Different theologians answer differently. Process theologians, theistic evolutionists, Intelligent Design proponents and creationists all draw different conclusions from the same biological consensus.

items.reflection: Darwin's 1859 book is one of the most consequential books ever written. Its impact on biology is fundamental and contested; its impact on theology and philosophy of religion has been profound. The interaction continues to shape religious thinking in the 21st century.

moments.title: Lemaitre proposes expanding universe
moments.who: Georges Lemaitre, Belgian Catholic priest and astronomer
moments.body: 1927: Lemaitre publishes (in French, in a Belgian journal) the first paper proposing an expanding universe with general relativity. He proposes that the universe expanded from a 'primeval atom' — what Fred Hoyle later mockingly called the 'Big Bang'.
moments.takeaway: Edwin Hubble's 1929 paper confirming galactic recession is often credited as the discovery; Lemaitre had the theoretical framework two years earlier.

moments.title: Einstein hears Lemaitre
moments.who: Einstein, Lemaitre, California Institute of Technology
moments.body: January 1933: Einstein attends Lemaitre's lecture at Mount Wilson. He had called Lemaitre's earlier work 'abominable physics' but now accepts the expanding universe. 'This is the most beautiful and satisfactory explanation of creation to which I have ever listened.'
moments.takeaway: Einstein's cosmological constant — introduced to keep the universe static — was abandoned. Decades later it would be revived to account for dark energy.

moments.title: Pope Pius XII's 'creation' claim
moments.body: November 1951: Pius XII addresses the Pontifical Academy of Sciences with a speech treating the Big Bang as confirmation of Genesis. Lemaitre — by then a senior figure in the Pontifical Academy — privately persuades the Pope not to make this claim again. Science and theology should not be conflated.
moments.takeaway: Lemaitre insisted his theory was scientific, neutral with respect to religious doctrine. The same evidence could be read by believers and non-believers in different ways.

now.title: Cosmology and faith
now.body: The Big Bang model has been overwhelmingly confirmed — cosmic microwave background (1964), light-element abundances, large-scale structure. Modern cosmology includes inflation, dark matter, dark energy and unsolved questions about origins. Theologians and philosophers of religion (William Lane Craig's Kalam cosmological argument) have engaged extensively.
now.open_questions: Does the Big Bang prove or disprove anything about God? Lemaitre's answer (neither) remains the responsible position. Different communities read the science differently.

items.reflection: A Catholic priest produced one of the most consequential theories in modern cosmology. Lemaitre's care to keep science and religion methodologically separate — even as he held both — is a model for engagement that more polarised contemporaries (on both sides) have struggled to maintain.

moments.title: Tractatus
moments.body: 1922: 'Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus' published. Famously: 'Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent' (7). Religion, ethics and aesthetics belong to the 'mystical' — the inexpressible.
moments.takeaway: Early Wittgenstein treated religious language as showing rather than saying — it points to what cannot be put into propositions.

moments.title: Lectures on Religious Belief
moments.body: 1938 Cambridge lectures on religious belief. Wittgenstein resists treating religious claims as scientific hypotheses or as straightforwardly true/false statements. The religious believer who says 'I believe in a Last Judgment' is not making the same kind of claim as a person predicting an event.
moments.takeaway: The 'language game' framework began to be applied to religion in these lectures. Religious utterances have their own grammar.

moments.title: Philosophical Investigations
moments.body: 1953: 'Philosophical Investigations' published posthumously. Language games and forms of life. D.Z. Phillips (1965 'The Concept of Prayer', and many later works) develops a Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion treating religious language as expressing a form of life rather than describing facts.
moments.takeaway: Wittgensteinian fideism (the term is sometimes pejorative) treats religious belief as a form of life with its own grammar — not requiring or admitting external evidence.

now.title: Wittgenstein's continuing influence
now.body: Modern Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion (D.Z. Phillips, Rush Rhees, more recently Stephen Mulhall) continues to develop the approach. Critics argue it makes religion immune from criticism; defenders argue it captures something true about how religious language actually functions.
now.open_questions: Is religious language descriptive, expressive or something else? Wittgensteinian, expressivist and realist accounts give different answers. The question is central to modern philosophy of religion.

items.reflection: A Cambridge philosopher's approach to language transformed philosophy of religion. Whether or not one accepts the Wittgensteinian conclusion, his attention to how religious language actually works has reshaped the field.

moments.title: Medellin
moments.body: August-September 1968: the Latin American bishops meet at Medellin, Colombia. The conference applies Vatican II to Latin American realities — endorsing the 'preferential option for the poor' and critiquing structural injustice.
moments.takeaway: Medellin opened the door for liberation theology. Vatican II's general framework was being applied to specific regional context.

moments.title: Gustavo Gutierrez's 'Liberation Theology'
moments.body: 1971: Gutierrez publishes 'Teología de la Liberación' (English 1973). Theology should start from the experience of the poor; salvation includes liberation from social and economic oppression as well as sin. Marxist analytical tools are used (with debate) to understand structural injustice.
moments.takeaway: Gutierrez became the most prominent liberation theologian. He survived investigations by the CDF in the 1980s but was never formally censured.

moments.title: Oscar Romero assassinated
moments.who: Archbishop Oscar Romero of San Salvador
moments.body: 24 March 1980: Romero is shot at the altar while saying Mass. He had become an outspoken critic of the El Salvadoran military government and death squads. His murder galvanises Latin American Catholic engagement with social justice.

quote.text: If they kill me, I will rise again in the Salvadoran people.
quote.attrib: Oscar Romero, 1980, days before his murder

moments.takeaway: Romero was canonised by Pope Francis in 2018. The arc from threat to saint took 38 years.

now.title: Liberation theology's legacy
now.body: John Paul II's pontificate was generally critical of Marxist-influenced liberation theology. Pope Francis (Argentinian, formed in Latin American Jesuit context) has been more sympathetic. Liberation theology now extends to feminist, Black, queer, ecological and post-colonial variants. The 'preferential option for the poor' is mainstream Catholic teaching.
now.open_questions: What is the future of liberation theology? Marxist frameworks have lost some intellectual force; the underlying concerns (poverty, injustice) remain. The framework continues to evolve.

items.reflection: A movement of Latin American Catholic theologians transformed Christianity's relationship with structural injustice. The combination of biblical theology, social analysis and political commitment shaped the church and the politics of an entire continent.

moments.title: Azusa Street Revival
moments.body: April 1906: African American preacher William J. Seymour leads a multi-racial revival at 312 Azusa Street, Los Angeles. Speaking in tongues, healings, prophecy. The interracial worship was radical in segregated America.
moments.takeaway: Azusa Street is the conventional starting point of global Pentecostalism. Within years missionaries had carried the message worldwide.

moments.title: Global spread
moments.body: Pentecostalism spreads rapidly — Brazil (Assembleias de Deus, 1911), Chile, the Caribbean, Africa, India. The Holiness churches, the Pentecostal denominations (Assemblies of God 1914, Church of God in Christ) develop institutional forms. The charismatic movement (1960s) brings Pentecostal practices into mainline denominations.
moments.takeaway: By 2000, perhaps a quarter of the world's Christians could be classified as Pentecostal or charismatic.

moments.title: Global South majority
moments.body: Late 20th century: Pentecostal Christianity grows fastest in the Global South. African Initiated Churches, Brazilian neo-Pentecostal megachurches (Universal Church of the Kingdom of God), Korean megachurches. The centre of gravity of world Christianity shifts south.
moments.takeaway: By 2050, around 70% of the world's Christians will live outside Europe and North America.

now.title: World Christianity reshaped
now.body: Pentecostal/charismatic Christianity is now the second-largest Christian tradition globally (Catholic first). The character is varied — neo-Pentecostal prosperity gospel (often criticised), classical Pentecostal denominations, charismatic movements within Catholicism and Anglicanism. The future of Christianity will be substantially Pentecostal.
now.open_questions: How will Global South Christianity reshape global Christianity? Theological agendas (sexuality, gender) often align differently from Northern liberal mainstream. Ecumenical relations are evolving.

items.reflection: A 1906 Los Angeles revival sparked the fastest-growing Christian movement of the 20th century. Pentecostalism's combination of experiential worship, biblical fundamentalism (in many forms) and indigenisation has remade the global religious landscape.

moments.title: Weber's Protestant Ethic
moments.body: 1905: 'The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism' published. Weber argues Calvinist theology (predestination, calling) shaped attitudes that enabled capitalism. The 'disenchantment of the world' (Entzauberung) is modernity's defining feature.
moments.takeaway: Weber's framework dominated 20th-century sociology of religion. The secularisation thesis — that modernisation produces declining religiosity — became almost paradigmatic.

moments.title: Secularisation thesis dominant
moments.who: Peter Berger, Bryan Wilson, David Martin
moments.body: Berger's 'The Sacred Canopy' (1967) presented the strong secularisation thesis. Wilson's 'Religion in Secular Society' (1966) framed the British case. Mass-cultural secularisation, declining attendance, the privatisation of religion — all seemed empirically clear in Europe.
moments.takeaway: The thesis fit 1960s-70s European data well. Application elsewhere (US, much of the Global South) was always more contested.

moments.title: Berger reverses
moments.body: 1999: Berger publishes 'The Desecularization of the World'. He acknowledges that worldwide, religion is not declining. The US, Pentecostal Christianity, Islam, Hindu nationalism all show vitality. Religious modernity (José Casanova) and 'multiple modernities' (Eisenstadt) reframe the question.
moments.takeaway: European secularisation may be exceptional rather than paradigmatic. Charles Taylor's 'A Secular Age' (2007) offers a more nuanced account.

now.title: Where secularisation works
now.body: UK 2021 census: Christianity down to 46.2%; no religion at 37.2%. Most European countries show similar patterns. The US 'nones' have grown to around 30%. Religion remains vital in much of the Global South. The 'secularisation thesis' has not been falsified but has been substantially complicated.
now.open_questions: Is religious decline reversible or terminal? Generational data suggests further decline; conversion data shows continued movement (in both directions). The question is empirically open.

items.reflection: The sociology of religion's central thesis was simpler than the evidence sustained. Religion's relationship to modernity varies across cultures, classes and generations. Modernity is not monolithic; nor is religion. The conversation continues.

moments.title: Vatican II opens
moments.body: October 1962: Vatican II begins. Among its documents, Nostra Aetate (1965) addressed non-Christian religions positively for the first time at this level. The Catholic Church engaged Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism as containing 'rays of truth'.
moments.takeaway: The shift from exclusivism to inclusivism in major Christian churches was a 20th-century event. Earlier centuries had been almost universally exclusivist.

moments.title: Pluralism theology
moments.body: Hick's 'God Has Many Names' (1980) and 'An Interpretation of Religion' (1989) develop pluralism — different religions are different culturally-conditioned responses to the same ultimate reality. Knitter's 'No Other Name?' (1985) and later works develop the Catholic version.
moments.takeaway: Three positions: exclusivism (only one religion is true), inclusivism (one is true but others contain truth), pluralism (many are equally valid). Hick is the canonical pluralist.

moments.title: Multi-faith Britain
moments.body: UK 2001 census introduced the religion question. Christians 71.7%, Muslims 3.0%, Hindus 1.0%, Sikhs 0.6%, Jews 0.5%, Buddhists 0.3%. By 2021: Christians 46.2%, Muslims 6.5%, Hindus 1.7%. Council of Christians and Jews (1942), Inter Faith Network (1987), local councils of faith map the institutional landscape.
moments.takeaway: Britain's religious landscape diversified rapidly in the postwar period through migration. The institutional response (RE curriculum, faith schools, interfaith bodies) developed over decades.

now.title: Living together
now.body: Modern Britain is religiously diverse and increasingly secular at once. Faith schools (still around 30% of state schools) coexist with declining religious affiliation. Interfaith dialogue, multi-faith chaplaincy, and religious literacy education are now standard. Tensions (over religious symbols, public worship, anti-Muslim and antisemitic prejudice) continue.
now.open_questions: How should religion appear in public life? Different European countries answer differently (French laïcité, UK established church, German Kirchensteuer system). The questions don't have one answer.

items.reflection: Modern religious pluralism is both empirical fact and theological challenge. The practical question — how do different religious communities live together — is now the major shared issue across traditions. Theology and policy are still catching up.

moments.title: The Fundamentals
moments.body: 1910-15: 'The Fundamentals: A Testimony to the Truth' — 12 volumes of essays defending traditional Protestant doctrine against liberal theology, biblical criticism and Darwinism. The term 'fundamentalist' was coined from this series.
moments.takeaway: Original Protestant fundamentalism is a particular early-20th-century American phenomenon. Its application to other religions is much later.

moments.title: Scopes trial
moments.who: John Scopes, William Jennings Bryan, Clarence Darrow
moments.body: July 1925: high school teacher John Scopes is tried in Dayton, Tennessee, for teaching evolution. Bryan prosecutes, Darrow defends. The trial becomes a national cultural event. Scopes is convicted (overturned on a technicality).
moments.takeaway: The trial damaged Protestant fundamentalism's public standing for a generation. The 1970s saw a major revival.

moments.title: Iranian Revolution and global Islamism
moments.body: 1979: the Iranian Revolution brings Khomeini's clerical Shia regime to power. The Iranian model and contemporary Sunni movements (Muslim Brotherhood, Wahhabism) are widely framed as 'Islamic fundamentalism'. The Fundamentalism Project (Marty and Appleby, 1991-95) develops a comparative framework.
moments.takeaway: Modern application of 'fundamentalism' across religions has been criticised by scholars (the term originated in a particular Protestant context). It nevertheless remains widely used.

now.title: Religious assertion in the modern world
now.body: Hindu nationalism (BJP, RSS), Christian Zionism, the religious right in Israel, Jewish ultra-Orthodoxy, Wahhabi Islam, evangelical political mobilisation in the US and Brazil — all variants of religious-conservative mobilisation in late modernity. Karen Armstrong's 'The Battle for God' (2000) is one synthesis.
now.open_questions: Is religious fundamentalism a reaction against modernity or a modern phenomenon in religious clothing? Both, in different proportions. Most fundamentalisms use modern media, modern political mobilisation, and modern ideological frameworks.

items.reflection: Religion didn't fade in the 20th century as many had predicted. Instead, militant traditionalism gained new energy across multiple religious traditions. The 21st century is finding new forms — but the dynamic of religious mobilisation against secular modernity is now a permanent feature of global politics.

moments.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion
moments.body: 1536: Calvin (then 26) publishes the first edition of his Institutes in Basel. Latin, six chapters. He revises and expands repeatedly through 1559 (final edition, 80 chapters). The Institutes become the central text of Reformed Protestantism.
moments.takeaway: Calvin's systematic theology shaped Presbyterian, Reformed and (later) much Baptist tradition. Predestination, double predestination, total depravity, perseverance of the saints — the TULIP framework comes from later Calvinist systematisation.

moments.title: Geneva as reformed model
moments.body: Calvin organises Geneva as a reformed city. Ecclesiastical Ordinances (1541) establish four offices: pastors, doctors, elders, deacons. Strict moral discipline through the consistory. Geneva becomes a refuge for Reformed Protestants across Europe (John Knox spent time there).
moments.takeaway: Geneva was the model for subsequent Reformed cities and the training ground for Reformed leaders. John Knox returned to Scotland in 1559 and led the Scottish Reformation.

moments.title: Servetus burned
moments.body: 27 October 1553: Michael Servetus — a Spanish anti-Trinitarian — is burned at the stake at Champel, Geneva. Calvin pushed for execution by sword (Servetus had escaped Catholic burning) but the council ordered burning. The case remains a difficult moment for Calvin's reputation.
moments.takeaway: Religious toleration was not yet a Protestant norm. Most Reformers accepted state coercion in matters of religion.

now.title: Reformed Christianity today
now.body: Reformed and Presbyterian churches have around 75 million adherents globally — concentrated in Scotland, the Netherlands, Hungary, South Korea, and various Reformed denominations elsewhere. Calvinist theology has experienced revival through neo-Calvinism (Dutch tradition: Kuyper, Bavinck) and contemporary American figures (R.C. Sproul, John Piper, 'New Calvinism').
now.open_questions: Is Calvin's theology coherent on free will and divine sovereignty? The question has been debated since the 16th century. Different solutions (compatibilism, hyper-Calvinism, Amyraldianism) recur.

items.reflection: A 26-year-old French exile in Basel wrote the systematic theology that shaped a major branch of Christianity. Calvin's Geneva model influenced political institutions (Scotland, parts of the Netherlands, New England) as much as theological tradition.

moments.title: Council of Trent
moments.body: 1545-1563: the Council of Trent meets in three periods (1545-47, 1551-52, 1562-63). It responds to the Protestant Reformation by defining Catholic doctrine clearly — on Scripture (Vulgate, tradition alongside Bible), justification (against Luther), the seven sacraments, the Mass as sacrifice, transubstantiation.
moments.takeaway: Trent's decrees defined Catholic identity for the next 400 years. The 'Counter-Reformation' framework was set.

moments.title: Reform implementation
moments.who: Council of Trent decrees, post-Tridentine bishops
moments.body: Seminaries for priestly formation, vernacular catechisms (Catechism of the Council of Trent 1566), liturgical standardisation (Roman Missal 1570), better-trained bishops resident in their dioceses. Charles Borromeo at Milan and others implemented the reform programme.
moments.takeaway: The 'Counter' part of Counter-Reformation overshadows the 'Catholic Reformation' aspect. Many of Trent's reforms had been called for before the Protestant rupture.

moments.title: Vatican II as second great reform
moments.body: 1962-65: Vatican II is the Catholic Church's first major council since Vatican I (1869-70). Its trajectory — vernacular liturgy, ecumenism, religious freedom, engagement with modernity — represents a major shift from the Tridentine framework that had operated since the 16th century.
moments.takeaway: The Tridentine Mass (1570 Roman Missal) was the standard until 1969. Pope Benedict XVI's 'Summorum Pontificum' (2007) eased restrictions on the older Mass; Pope Francis (2021) restricted it again.

now.title: Tridentine inheritance
now.body: Catholic doctrine on sacraments, justification, ecclesiology and biblical interpretation has its modern form substantially from Trent. The reforms of Vatican II are best understood as building on Trent rather than replacing it. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992) draws on both councils.
now.open_questions: How should Trent be read after Vatican II? Continuity (Benedict's 'hermeneutic of continuity'), reform (most modern theology), or rupture (some progressives, some traditionalists). The question shapes contemporary Catholic identity politics.

items.reflection: A 16th-century council defined Catholic identity in opposition to Protestantism. Its decrees shaped the church for four centuries. The major recent reform (Vatican II) has been read as either continuous or discontinuous with Trent — the disagreement itself shows how foundational the older council was.

moments.title: Great Awakenings
moments.who: George Whitefield, John Wesley, Jonathan Edwards
moments.body: 1730s-40s: revivals across the British Atlantic. Wesley's Methodism, Whitefield's preaching, Edwards's 'Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God' (1741). The Awakenings produced the emphasis on personal conversion, biblical authority, evangelism that defines evangelicalism.
moments.takeaway: Evangelicalism as a term has 18th-century roots in the Awakenings. The modern phenomenon descends from this.

moments.title: National Association of Evangelicals
moments.body: 1942: NAE founded to provide moderate evangelical alternatives to fundamentalism. Carl F. H. Henry's 'The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism' (1947) called for evangelical social engagement. Billy Graham's New York crusade (1957) marked the postwar emergence.
moments.takeaway: Postwar 'neo-evangelicalism' distinguished itself from fundamentalism by greater intellectual engagement and ecumenical breadth — while sharing core convictions.

moments.title: Religious Right and global evangelicalism
moments.who: Falwell's Moral Majority, Robertson's Christian Coalition, global expansion
moments.body: 1979: Jerry Falwell founds Moral Majority. The Religious Right becomes a major US political force through Reagan, Bush, Trump eras. Globally, evangelical and Pentecostal Christianity grow rapidly in Latin America, Africa, East Asia. African Anglicanism, Brazilian neo-Pentecostalism, Chinese house churches.
moments.takeaway: By 2000s, evangelicalism is global. The American political variant is a small share of the worldwide phenomenon.

now.title: World evangelicalism
now.body: David Bebbington's 'evangelical quadrilateral' (biblicism, crucicentrism, conversionism, activism) remains a standard definition. World Evangelical Alliance estimates 600 million evangelicals globally. The American political alignment, the Brazilian prosperity gospel, the African Anglican traditionalism are all part of one phenomenon — broadly.
now.open_questions: Has American evangelicalism become primarily political? Post-2016, a substantial debate has run about whether the movement has been captured by Trumpist politics. Russell Moore, Beth Moore and others have departed in protest. The category remains contested.

items.reflection: Evangelical Christianity is one of the largest religious phenomena of late modernity. Its combination of personal religion, biblical authority and missionary outreach has produced rapid global growth — and its political entanglements in the US have produced the most contested form.

moments.title: Early Sufism
moments.body: 8th-10th centuries: Sufism emerges as Islamic mysticism. Hasan al-Basri (d. 728), Rabia al-Adawiyya (d. 801, the great female mystic), al-Junayd of Baghdad (d. 910) develop the tradition. Mansur al-Hallaj (executed 922 for his statement 'Ana al-haqq' — 'I am the truth') represents the controversial wing.
moments.takeaway: Sufism developed alongside, sometimes in tension with, Islamic legalism (sharia). Al-Ghazali's reconciliation (11th c.) would be central.

moments.title: Tariqas and Rumi
moments.body: 12th-13th c.: Sufi orders (tariqas) develop — Qadiriyya, Suhrawardiyya, Naqshbandiyya, Mevleviyya. Jalaluddin Rumi (1207-1273) of Konya writes the Masnavi, one of the great works of Persian literature and Sufi poetry. The Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes' descend from his community.

quote.text: Come, come, whoever you are. Wanderer, worshipper, lover of leaving. Ours is not a caravan of despair.
quote.attrib: Often attributed to Rumi (translation issues; the spirit is genuinely Sufi)

moments.takeaway: Rumi has been one of America's bestselling poets in recent decades — through translations sometimes disputed for their faithfulness to the original Sufi context.

moments.title: Sufism contested
moments.body: From the 18th c., reformist movements (Wahhabism in Arabia, Salafism more broadly) have often opposed Sufi practices as innovation (bid'a). Modernist Sufism (Inayat Khan in the West, 1910s) reaches non-Muslim audiences. The Mevlevi order's whirling ceremony is now UNESCO-recognised heritage.
moments.takeaway: Sufi shrines remain pilgrimage sites across the Muslim world. Reformist demolitions (Saudi Arabia, Mali under Ansar Dine) have destroyed some. Sufism remains broadly popular at folk level.

now.title: Mysticism in the modern world
now.body: Sufism reaches Western audiences through Rumi translations, world music (qawwali singers like Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan), academic study and converts. In majority-Muslim societies, it remains contested — orthodox revival has sometimes targeted Sufi practices.
now.open_questions: Is Sufism a separate Islamic tradition or a dimension within Islam? Most Sufis insist on the latter; reformists often treat it as deviation. Different Muslim societies answer differently.

items.reflection: Islamic mysticism developed alongside, sometimes within tension with, Islamic legalism. The two are now widely treated as complementary by mainstream Sunni and Shia scholarship — though contested by reformist movements. Rumi's contemporary global readership shows the universality of the Sufi message.

moments.title: First sermon at Sarnath
moments.body: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta ('Setting the Wheel of Dharma in Motion') is delivered in the Deer Park at Sarnath. The Buddha teaches the Four Noble Truths: there is dukkha (suffering, unsatisfactoriness); the cause is craving (tanha); cessation is possible; the Noble Eightfold Path leads there.
moments.takeaway: The Eightfold Path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration. The 'middle way' between asceticism and indulgence.

moments.title: Pali Canon written
moments.body: Around 100 BCE, the Buddhist teachings — preserved orally for 400 years — are first written down at Aluvihara in Sri Lanka, possibly during a famine that threatened the chain of oral transmission. The Tipitaka (Three Baskets) contains Vinaya (monastic discipline), Sutta (discourses), and Abhidhamma (philosophical analysis).
moments.takeaway: The Pali Canon remains the canonical scriptures for Theravada Buddhism. Mahayana traditions added many more sutras (Lotus, Heart, Diamond, Pure Land).

moments.title: Engaged Buddhism
moments.who: Thich Nhat Hanh, the Dalai Lama, B.R. Ambedkar
moments.body: Thich Nhat Hanh's 'Engaged Buddhism' (term coined 1960s) applies Buddhist principles to social action. B.R. Ambedkar leads the Dalit mass conversion to Buddhism in 1956. The 14th Dalai Lama goes into Indian exile in 1959 and becomes a global figure.
moments.takeaway: Modern Buddhism has had to engage colonialism, modernity, science, and political conflict in ways the early sangha didn't anticipate.

now.title: Buddhism in the modern world
now.body: Around 500 million Buddhists globally. Mindfulness practices (MBSR, MBCT) have entered mainstream Western healthcare and education. Theravada (Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar), Mahayana (China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam) and Vajrayana (Tibet, Mongolia) all flourish in different forms. Secular Buddhism (Stephen Batchelor) is a growing tendency.
now.open_questions: What is the Buddha's actual teaching? Some scholars argue the Pali Canon's earliest material reaches close; others that all our texts are later compositions. The historical Buddha is harder to access than the textual Buddha.

items.reflection: The Four Noble Truths frame human life as a problem with a solution. The diagnosis (suffering caused by craving) and treatment (eightfold path) form a complete therapy. Their continued global appeal — across radically different cultural contexts — testifies to their depth.

moments.title: Bodhidharma in China
moments.body: Around 520 CE, the Indian monk Bodhidharma reaches China and (according to tradition) meditates facing a wall at Shaolin temple for nine years. He becomes the first patriarch of Chan (Zen) Buddhism in China. The early Chan tradition emphasises sudden insight rather than gradual cultivation.
moments.takeaway: Chan emerged from interaction between Indian Mahayana Buddhism and Chinese Daoist tradition. The Northern (gradual) and Southern (sudden) schools split in the 8th century — the Southern won.

moments.title: Dogen and Soto Zen
moments.body: Dogen studied in China and returned to Japan in 1227. His Shobogenzo ('Treasury of the True Dharma Eye') is a masterpiece of Buddhist philosophy. Founded Soto Zen, emphasising 'just sitting' (shikantaza). Eiheiji monastery (1244) remains a centre.
moments.takeaway: Rinzai Zen (Eisai, 1141-1215) emphasises koan study and sudden enlightenment; Soto (Dogen) emphasises gradual practice through seated meditation. Both flourish in Japan.

moments.title: Zen reaches the West
moments.who: D. T. Suzuki, Alan Watts, Beat Generation
moments.body: D. T. Suzuki's English-language books popularised Zen for Western readers from the 1930s. Alan Watts's 'The Way of Zen' (1957) reached mass audiences. The Beat Generation (Kerouac's 'Dharma Bums', 1958), then 1960s counterculture, embraced Zen. Shunryu Suzuki founded San Francisco Zen Center (1969).
moments.takeaway: Western Zen has often been criticised as a stripped-down version of the tradition. But it has also produced serious lineages and original teachers.

now.title: Zen now
now.body: Zen continues to be practised globally — Asian heritage communities, established Western Zen centres, increasingly Latin American lineages. Mindfulness (much of which traces partly to Zen practice via secular adaptation) has reached very wide audiences. Critique of 'McMindfulness' has accompanied the wave.
now.open_questions: Is secular mindfulness still Buddhist? The line between Buddhist meditation and contextless practice is contested. Some traditional teachers worry about decontextualisation; others welcome the wider reach.

items.reflection: A meditation tradition that travelled from India to China to Japan to the West has reshaped global understanding of contemplative practice. Zen's combination of direct insight, koan study and disciplined sitting has spoken to seekers across radically different cultures.

moments.title: Alvars and Nayanars
moments.body: 6th-9th c.: the Alvars (Vaishnava) and Nayanars (Shaiva) compose passionate devotional poetry in Tamil. They reject caste distinctions, ritual exclusivism and Sanskrit-only orthodoxy. Their songs to Vishnu/Krishna and Shiva define South Indian devotional tradition.
moments.takeaway: Bhakti began in the Tamil south. The Sangam tradition and Dravidian languages were central to its development.

moments.title: Northern bhakti
moments.body: Bhakti spreads north in waves. Ramanuja (11th c.) systematises Vaishnava bhakti theology. Kabir (15th c.) writes ecstatic poetry uniting Hindu and Sufi sensibilities. Mirabai (16th c.) — Rajput princess — sings of her devotion to Krishna. Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas (1574) is a Hindi version of the Ramayana that becomes North India's defining text.

quote.text: My love for the Dark Lord is unbreakable.

moments.takeaway: Bhakti broke caste hierarchies in many of its expressions — Kabir, Mirabai, the Sant tradition. Modern Indian religious culture has deep bhakti roots.

moments.title: Chaitanya and Gaudiya Vaishnavism
moments.body: Chaitanya (1486-1534) of Bengal teaches ecstatic devotion to Krishna through chanting (kirtan), particularly the Hare Krishna mantra. His followers form Gaudiya Vaishnavism — the tradition from which ISKCON (1965, A.C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada) derives.
moments.takeaway: Modern global Krishna devotion — through ISKCON's outreach — traces back to Chaitanya. The Hare Krishna chant is now globally familiar.

now.title: Devotion in modern Hinduism
now.body: Bhakti traditions remain vibrant — temple worship, mass pilgrimages (Kumbh Mela), Krishna devotion globally through ISKCON, popular Hindi cinema with Bhakti themes. Bhakti remains the dominant religious mode for most Hindu lay people, alongside ritual and philosophical traditions.
now.open_questions: Does bhakti challenge caste or accommodate it? Many bhakti saints rejected caste in principle; the historical impact has been more limited than the rhetoric. The question remains live in modern Indian religious politics.

items.reflection: The bhakti movement reshaped Indian religious life across centuries. Its democratising impulse, its passionate poetry and its emphasis on personal devotion have proven among the most durable currents in Hinduism — and have shaped how non-Hindus encounter the tradition.

moments.title: Jewish dialogue begins
moments.body: 1960: French Jewish historian Jules Isaac meets Pope John XXIII. Isaac, whose family was murdered in Auschwitz, presents the historical case against Christian 'teaching of contempt' for Judaism. John XXIII commits to addressing the question at the coming council.
moments.takeaway: The Holocaust and individual relationships drove the dramatic shift in Catholic-Jewish dialogue at Vatican II.

moments.title: Nostra Aetate promulgated
moments.who: Paul VI and the Council Fathers
moments.body: 28 October 1965: 'Nostra Aetate' is promulgated. It rejects the collective Jewish guilt charge for Christ's death, condemns antisemitism, treats Judaism with respect as continuing covenant people, and engages Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism positively.

quote.text: The church... decries hatreds, persecutions, displays of antisemitism, directed against Jews at any time and by anyone.

moments.takeaway: The shortest of Vatican II's documents has been one of the most consequential. Nearly 2,000 years of Catholic-Jewish relations were redirected.

moments.title: Papal visits to synagogue and Yad Vashem
moments.body: April 1986: John Paul II becomes the first Pope to visit a synagogue (Rome's Great Synagogue) in modern times. March 2000: he visits Yad Vashem and the Western Wall during a Holy Land pilgrimage. The Vatican established diplomatic relations with Israel in 1993.
moments.takeaway: Symbolic acts continued the institutional shift. Pope Francis has built on the framework.

now.title: 60 years on
now.body: Catholic-Jewish dialogue is now institutional. The International Catholic-Jewish Liaison Committee (since 1971), the Pontifical Commission for Religious Relations with the Jews (1974), and bilateral conversations have produced sustained engagement. Antisemitism in the broader culture (including Catholic-majority countries) remains a concern.
now.open_questions: How should the church handle its historical record? Acts of public penance (John Paul II's 'Day of Pardon', March 2000) and academic engagement (Vatican archives opening for Pius XII era) continue.

items.reflection: A short conciliar document reshaped 2,000 years of Catholic-Jewish history. The shift was driven by individual relationships, the trauma of the Holocaust, and theological reflection — and has produced one of the major interfaith successes of the modern era.

moments.title: Ibn Sina (Avicenna)
moments.body: Ibn Sina writes the Kitab al-Shifa (The Book of Healing) — vast philosophical encyclopedia — and the Qanun fi al-Tibb (Canon of Medicine), the standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world for centuries. His theological work develops the distinction between essence and existence.
moments.takeaway: Avicenna is the first major philosopher to make essence-existence distinction central. Aquinas's 'esse' theology builds on this.

moments.title: Al-Ghazali
moments.body: Al-Ghazali's intellectual crisis at the height of his career (around 1095) led him to leave his teaching post in Baghdad. His 'Incoherence of the Philosophers' (Tahafut al-falasifa, c. 1095) critiques Avicennan philosophy from a theological standpoint. His 'Ihya Ulum al-Din' (Revival of Religious Sciences) integrates Sufism with mainstream Sunni orthodoxy.

quote.text: I knew that what brought me to leave Baghdad was a divine concern.

moments.takeaway: Al-Ghazali's reconciliation of Sufism with sharia-based orthodoxy was decisive for subsequent Sunni Islam.

moments.title: Ibn Rushd (Averroes)
moments.body: Ibn Rushd's 'Incoherence of the Incoherence' (Tahafut al-Tahafut) replies to al-Ghazali. He defends Aristotle and the philosophers. His commentaries on Aristotle are translated into Latin and shape European scholasticism. In the Islamic world, his influence faded after his death.
moments.takeaway: Averroes's afterlife was largely in the Christian West. Aquinas referred to him simply as 'the Commentator'.

now.title: Islamic philosophy today
now.body: Modern revivals of Islamic philosophy — Mohammed Iqbal's 'Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam' (1930), Ali Shariati in pre-revolutionary Iran, contemporary figures like Tariq Ramadan and Ziauddin Sardar — continue the tradition. The relationship between revealed knowledge and rational inquiry remains live.
now.open_questions: Why did the Islamic philosophical tradition decline after al-Ghazali? The thesis is contested. George Saliba and others argue scientific and philosophical work continued well into the early modern period; decline began later.

items.reflection: Islamic philosophy was a major engine of medieval intellectual life — and the bridge that returned Aristotle to Latin Europe. Its modern revival is part of the broader conversation about Islamic modernity and tradition.

moments.title: Either/Or and Fear and Trembling
moments.body: 1843: Kierkegaard publishes 'Either/Or' (the aesthetic vs. ethical life) and 'Fear and Trembling' (Abraham's binding of Isaac). The latter analyses Abraham as 'knight of faith' — willing to suspend ethics for divine command. The 'teleological suspension of the ethical' is one of the most discussed concepts in modern theology.
moments.takeaway: Kierkegaard wrote under pseudonyms and in many genres. Direct attribution of 'his' views to him is complicated by design.

moments.title: Philosophical Fragments and The Concept of Anxiety
moments.body: 1844: 'Philosophical Fragments' (under Johannes Climacus pseudonym) argues the central religious claim — the eternal entering time in Christ — is absurd by reason yet calls for faith. 'The Concept of Anxiety' (Vigilius Haufniensis) analyses anxiety as the 'dizziness of freedom'.
moments.takeaway: Kierkegaard prefigures 20th-century existentialism — Heidegger, Sartre, Camus — though they often drew different conclusions.

moments.title: Attack on Christendom
moments.body: Kierkegaard's late 'Attack upon Christendom' (1854-55) tears into the Danish state church for confusing cultural Christianity with genuine discipleship. He dies in 1855, aged 42, having spent his inheritance on books and pamphlets.
moments.takeaway: The critique of 'Christendom' — Christianity reduced to social convention — has influenced Bonhoeffer, Karl Barth, the entire 20th-century Protestant theological renewal.

now.title: Kierkegaard's reach
now.body: Karl Barth, Dietrich Bonhoeffer, Paul Tillich, Reinhold Niebuhr, Rudolf Bultmann — much 20th-century Protestant theology bears Kierkegaardian inheritance. Modern Christian existentialism, religious phenomenology and post-secular theology continue to engage him. Each generation rediscovers him.
now.open_questions: Is Kierkegaardian faith rational? The 'leap of faith' has been read as fideistic (reason fails, jump anyway) and as something more complex (reason and faith are different modes). Both readings have textual support.

items.reflection: A 19th-century Danish writer launching attacks on the established church became one of the most influential modern religious thinkers. Kierkegaard's combination of psychological depth, philosophical seriousness and theological commitment remade Protestant theology — and prefigured existentialism.

moments.title: Aquinas writes the Five Ways
moments.body: Aquinas's Five Ways (Quinque Viae) appear in Summa Theologiae I.2.3, occupying about a page. 1: motion (unmoved mover). 2: causation (uncaused first cause). 3: contingency (necessary being). 4: degrees (greatest being). 5: design (intelligent designer).
moments.takeaway: Aquinas presented the Ways as gestures toward a more developed natural theology, not stand-alone proofs. Modern apologetic use often isolates them from their original setting.

moments.title: Modern critiques
moments.body: Hume's Dialogues (1779) critiques the design argument. Kant (1781) argues that pure reason cannot prove God's existence — the cosmological and design arguments illegitimately apply categories of experience beyond experience. Both shape modern philosophy of religion.
moments.takeaway: The 'natural theology' tradition was on the defensive in the 19th century — and substantially revived in the 20th.

moments.title: Cosmological argument revived
moments.body: William Lane Craig's Kalam cosmological argument (developed from medieval Islamic sources): the universe began to exist; whatever begins to exist has a cause; therefore the universe has a cause. The Big Bang cosmology is presented as supporting the kalam premise. Edward Feser defends classical Thomist versions.
moments.takeaway: Contemporary natural theology (Plantinga, Swinburne, Craig, Feser) remains active. Whether the arguments are persuasive depends on prior commitments.

now.title: Arguments under examination
now.body: The Five Ways remain on every A-level Religious Studies syllabus. Modern atheistic responses (Bertrand Russell, Richard Dawkins) and theistic defences (Craig, Plantinga) coexist. The question — does any argument prove God's existence? — has been continuously discussed for 800 years.
now.open_questions: Do classical arguments work? Critics argue Hume and Kant settled the matter; defenders argue modern modal logic and cosmology have revived the arguments. The debate isn't resolvable empirically.

items.reflection: A 13th-century page in the Summa generated more philosophical work than almost any other equivalent text. The Five Ways remain a touchstone for thinking about the relationship between rational inquiry and religious belief.

moments.title: Sermon on the Mount
moments.body: Matthew's Gospel (chapters 5-7) records Jesus's longest single block of ethical teaching. Beatitudes ('Blessed are the poor in spirit...'), the antitheses ('You have heard that it was said... But I say to you...'), the Lord's Prayer, teaching on judgment, anxiety, possessions. Luke's Sermon on the Plain (Luke 6) is a parallel.
moments.takeaway: Whether Matthew 5-7 is one historical sermon or a composed collection of teachings, it functions as the heart of Christian ethical teaching.

moments.title: Augustine's interpretation
moments.who: Augustine, 'On the Sermon on the Mount'
moments.body: Augustine (in 'De Sermone Domini in Monte', c. 393-396) treats the Sermon as a complete summary of Christian moral life. The interpretive frame — Sermon as Christian ethics — has dominated subsequently.
moments.takeaway: The Sermon's centrality is a patristic decision as much as a feature of the text. Other gospel sections could have been similarly canonised.

moments.title: Bonhoeffer and 'cheap grace'
moments.body: Bonhoeffer's reading: the Sermon is not impossible idealism but the actual calling of the disciple. 'Cheap grace' — forgiveness without repentance, salvation without commitment — is the enemy. The Sermon demands what it demands.

quote.text: When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.
quote.attrib: Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship, 1937

moments.takeaway: Bonhoeffer was executed by the Nazis in 1945. His own life embodied his exegesis.

now.title: Living the Sermon
now.body: The Sermon continues to be central — to Christian preaching, to Tolstoy's pacifism, to Gandhi's non-violence (he read it constantly), to Martin Luther King's strategy, to monastic and lay Christian movements. Anabaptist and pacifist traditions read it as binding; mainline traditions interpret it variously.
now.open_questions: Was Jesus a literal pacifist? Mennonites, Quakers and some Catholics say yes; others see hyperbolic teaching that doesn't preclude just war. The exegetical question continues.

items.reflection: A series of teachings recorded by one early Christian community has become one of the most influential ethical texts in world history. Its actual content — radical love of enemies, indifference to possessions, focus on the kingdom — continues to challenge readers in every generation.
